item.title: Separating Pseudorandom Codes from Quantum Random Oracles
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2774
Authors: Nico Döttling, Anne Müller, Mahesh Sreekumar Rajasree
Summary: Pseudorandom codes (PRCs) combine two seemingly conflicting goals: robustness to noise and computational indistinguishability from random strings. Recent work has shown that classical symmetric-key PRCs over binary alphabets cannot be constructed from minimal cryptographic assumptions, such as one-way functions, via black-box reductions. In this work, we revisit this question in the presence of quantum computation and quantum information. We first consider pseudorandom codes with classical codewords but quantum algorithms. We prove that symmetric-key pseudorandom codes robust to Bernoulli noise admit no black-box construction from quantum random oracles, and hence from quantum-secure one-way functions. This establishes that the classical black-box barrier for PRCs persists even in the quantum computational setting. Motivated by this separation, we investigate the notion of quantum pseudorandom codes (QPRCs), in which codewords are quantum states and security is defined via computational indistinguishability from Haar-random states. We then present several positive results. Assuming quantum-secure one-way functions, we construct QPRCs that are secure against a single encoding query, allow multiple copies of the challenge state, and tolerate an error rate matching that of any classical uniquely decodable binary error-correcting code against a dephasing or bit-flip channel. We also show that the PRFS with proof of destruction due to Behera et al. (TCC 2023) can be extended to a 0-bit QPRC that is secure against multiple encoding queries and tolerates unbounded phase errors but only a constant number of bit-flip errors. Finally, assuming the existence of quantum-secure single-query pseudorandom states (1PRS), we construct single-query single-copy QPRC that tolerate arbitrary Pauli noise up to the decoding radius of a quantum error-correcting code with unique decoding.

item.title: Vectorized (2, 2)-Isogenies in the Theta Model Using AVX-512 and Applications to SQIsign
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2773
Authors: Marius A. Aardal, Diego F. Aranha, Patrick Longa, Giacomo Pope
Summary: Higher-dimensional isogenies have emerged as a powerful building block for isogeny-based cryptography, with recent protocols such as SQIsign relying on the efficient evaluation of $(2^n, 2^n)$-isogenies. Despite their attractive security and compactness properties, these schemes remain computationally expensive and improving their performance is an important step for their real-world use. In this work, we present a high-performance AVX-512 implementation of two-dimensional isogenies that effectively exploits their data-level parallelism. We develop a code generator that produces efficient AVX-512 implementations of arithmetic over $\mathbb{F}_p$ and $\mathbb{F}_{p^2}$ for Montgomery-friendly primes of the form $p=c\cdot 2^e-1$ with $e\approx \log_2(p)$, covering the family of primes used by several protocols based on two-dimensional isogenies, including SQIsign. Building on this arithmetic, we vectorize the $(2^n, 2^n)$-isogeny formulas by Dartois et al. (ASIACRYPT 2024), achieving significant speedups over the corresponding, highly-optimized scalar implementation that uses x86-64 assembly. As an application, we accelerate the Round 2 version of SQIsign verification and obtain speedups of $2.5\times$ at NIST security level I and $3.2\times$ and $3.3\times$ at levels III and V, respectively. Our code generator also readily supports the larger primes of Round 3 SQIsign, for which we obtain verification speedups between $3.1\times$ and $3.4\times$.

item.title: STIR/SHAKEN: A Cocktail of Cryptographic Clumsiness
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2772
Authors: Josh Brown, Matthew Hardeman, Paul Grubbs
Summary: Scams and fraudulent robocalls are rampant in the telephone system. Fraudsters often employ call spoofing to impersonate a known caller to the victim, making it difficult to detect and block the fraudster’s calls. In an effort to combat call spoofing, the U.S. government in 2019 mandated the use of a new suite of protocols called STIR/SHAKEN. In STIR/SHAKEN, providers include a cryptographically-signed assertion about the caller’s identity and other metadata in call headers. This serves both to authentically convey this metadata between providers during call routing and to provide reportable, verifiable evidence of bad behavior by providers that originate fraudulent calls. This paper asks whether STIR/SHAKEN achieves its security goals, and at what cost to the telephone system. On security we find serious structural weaknesses: a year of STIR/SHAKEN certificates observed in production call traffic shows a PKI riddled with noncompliance—nearly half of valid certificates violate the specifications—a provider can prevent later verification of a STIR/SHAKEN assertion by taking its certificate offline, and a header-malleability flaw, which we verified in test calls placed with the help of a real telephone provider, causes a spoofed caller ID to be displayed as verified on some phones. The cost, meanwhile, has been steep: STIR/SHAKEN deployment has created systemic new harms to the privacy of all phone users. These new privacy harms take two forms. First, signing call metadata renders it cryptographically non-repudiable: for the first time in the phone system’s 150-year history, there is publicly verifiable proof that a call took place. Second, STIR/SHAKEN’s complexity pushes providers to outsource signing and verification—roughly half of the 29 providers we surveyed do so, most to a handful of dominant vendors—causing widespread new leakage of sensitive call metadata to off-path third parties. (One such off-path third party, Neustar, was acquired in 2021 by TransUnion, one of the three nationwide U.S. credit bureaus. Neustar authenticates over 30 billion calls per month—and TransUnion sells a “Phone Behavior Intelligence” product advertising “insight into billions of call transactions” obtained through its “deep carrier relationships.”) These structural harms sit atop implementation failures: our tests also found implementations that completely break the federally-mandated *67 caller-privacy mechanism. Finally, we propose solutions to the problems we identify. To fix the PKI, STIR/SHAKEN should adopt certificate transparency; a public certificate log also stops providers from taking certificates offline to defeat later verification. Our remaining solutions are cryptographic, and share a prerequisite STIR/SHAKEN cannot currently meet: the origin provider must learn the destination provider’s public key. We thus design a backwards-compatible key discovery mechanism that uses SIP error messages. We then attack the privacy harms directly: replacing STIR/SHAKEN’s signatures with asymmetric message franking (AMF) makes call metadata deniable again, and issuing AMFs blindly keeps it hidden from outsourced signers. We design the first blind signing protocol for the AMF construction of Tyagi et al., along with new security definitions capturing requirements novel to the setting, such as verifier-hiding blindness. To our knowledge, we thereby initiate the formal study of blind signing for designated-verifier signatures; we believe this is of independent interest.

item.title: Can Fully Homomorphic Encryption on Public Blockchains Protect Sensitive Medical Consultations? A Security and Privacy Assessment
Sumcheck bit packing
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2770
Authors: Matteo Frigo, abhi shelat
Summary: Circuit-based zero-knowledge proofs over large fields waste most of a field element when they commit to a single bit. We study the problem of committing to packed witnesses, in which $m$ bits are stored in one element of $GF(2^m)$, while still allowing the proof system to verify linear claims about the individual bits.
Prior approaches to this problem either (a) scale to packing only 4 bits[Fs24], (b) require tensor-structured claims and additional sumcheck rounds that incur larger soundness error [DP23,DP25], or (c) rely on Frobenius automorphisms [Koc26]. In contrast, we present a simpler reduction that exploits only the $GF(2)$-linearity of the field trace and achieves soundness error $2^{-m}$ for arbitrary bit-linear claims. We then use a characterization of trace-zero field elements to make the reduction zero-knowledge over any hiding linear commitment scheme: whereas previous constructions verify $O(m^2)$ or $O(m)$quadratic constraints in the commitment scheme, our protocol requires only linear constraints.

item.title: Projective Jet Geometry and Hold-Out Rank of Binary Goppa Codes
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2769
Authors: Yongge Wang
Summary: We develop a projective-geometric and algebraic framework for the higher-order polynomial relations among the public generator-matrix columns of a binary Goppa code, the relations exploited by the recent structural distinguishers and key-recovery methods for Classic McEliece. The alternant representation realizes the public columns as rational points on a hidden curve parametrized over $\F_{2^m}$; higher-order vanishing conditions become fat-point conditions, pulled back along the hidden parametrization.
Our first contribution is an exact characterization of a codimension-$t$ ambient space containing all products of $d$ code polynomials: the products satisfy $(\pi^dh)'\equiv0\pmod{g^2}$ for the support polynomial $\pi$ and the Goppa polynomial $g$, and the space of degree-$\le dD$ polynomials with this property has dimension $dD+1-t$ once $dD\ge2t-1$. Equality with the actual product space is proved in a local regime, verified computationally on every instance tested, and stated as a conjecture. Our second contribution is a Frobenius-descent theorem: a binary form vanishes on the hidden curve if and only if it vanishes on the union of its $m$ Frobenius conjugates, with the $\F_2$-dimension of such forms equal to the $K$-dimension of the ideal of the union; from it we derive Hilbert-function bounds, including a multilinear version attained on all but one of the twenty-seven keys with $t\ge5$ tested (and missed by one on that key), and the local structure of the pulled-back forms at the roots of $g$.
We then analyze the universal dependencies among Hasse-jet conditions in the multilinear setting of the attacks: a closed formula for the rank at a single column, and an explicit family of $\binom{k}{2s-d-2}$ relations between the conditions at any two columns. At a held-out column we prove an exact codimension formula for the Goppa subcode generated by the gradients of the vanishing forms. Finally, running our experimental pipeline (the jet system of the attacks, without the key-recovery steps) on six independently generated keys of a Classic-McEliece-shaped code shows that the kernel dimension is comparable to that of a random control, while every kernel form exhibits the predicted hidden-curve vanishing, the gradients span the predicted subcode, and the first-order normal data of the kernel is nearly independent of the key. Together these results explain the main components of the nuisance space of the recent attacks and isolate the conjectures that remain for an exact description of the kernel.

item.title: HqcLethe: Streaming HQC Encapsulation for Tiny Stateless Servers
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2767
Authors: Wind Wong, Klaus v. Gleissenthall
Summary: Stateless post-quantum authenticated key exchanges such as post-quantum WireGuard hedge against unexpected cryptanalytic advances by combining a lattice KEM with code-based Classic McEliece. However, recent attacks have led Germany's BSI to advise against McEliece, which leaves these protocols with lattices alone. HQC, the code-based KEM that NIST selected, could restore diversity, but its keys do not fit in a single packet, so a server would have to buffer multi-packet handshakes. This would leave an attack surface for memory exhaustion, which is what WireGuard's stateless handshake was designed to avoid in the first place. McTiny demonstrated that stateless key encapsulation for Classic McEliece is possible by streaming key blocks one-at-a-time. However, HQC's encapsulation does not split as easily into individual packets, as cyclic polynomial multiplication, unlike matrix-vector multiplication, is inherently non-local.
We present HqcLethe, a stateless key exchange that streams an HQC encapsulation in packet-sized pieces. It uses the Chinese remainder theorem to split the polynomial multiplication into independent remainders, one per packet, and masks them so that they reveal no more than an ordinary HQC ciphertext, which we prove in Rocq with SSProve; we also verify session secrecy, server authentication and forward secrecy in ProVerif. Client puzzles bound CPU exhaustion, and HqcLethe removes memory exhaustion: on a Raspberry Pi 3B+, each worker runs in a fixed 1.2-1.6 MiB. At category 5 it sends 27x fewer bytes and uses 9.0x less server CPU than McTiny, the earlier stateless code-based design.

item.title: Keyber: Recovering the Signal by Amplifying the Noise in ML-KEM
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2766
Authors: Vipin Kumar, Prathamesh Ram, Suparna Kundu, Dhiman Saha
Summary: ML-KEM (FIPS 203) is now being deployed in real-world applications to provide security against adversaries with quantum computers. Therefore, the resistance of ML-KEM’s implementations to physical attacks requires thorough evaluation. So far, fault attacks on ML-KEM have targeted the decapsulation operation. The key generation operation has received little attention from a fault-attack perspective.
In this work, we present Keyber, the first statistical ineffective fault attack (SIFA) on the key generation of ML-KEM. Keyber is a key-recovery attack that needs only a single fault in key generation. The fault adds a known value to the error vector. Thus, the public key becomes faulty, while the seed of the public matrix remains intact. Every subsequent decapsulation, therefore, carries a known induced error. The adversary encapsulates locally and keeps only ciphertexts whose induced error peaks at exactly one coefficient. A decapsulation failure can then be attributed to that coefficient. Each query yields one linear inequality on the secret key, with no further faults.
We observe that approximately 0.2-27% of encapsulations are usable for different parameter sets of ML-KEM. The full secret key is recovered using up to 30,000 inequalities across all security levels. We also realise the attack for ML-KEM-512 on an ARM Cortex-M4 device using a single over-clock fault. We then recover the entire secret key end-to-end. A single fault in this one-time operation thus compromises the key for its entire lifetime. Protecting ML-KEM, therefore, demands hardening not only decapsulation, but also key generation.

item.title: Cryptanalysis of Pairing-Based Additive Masking with Prime-Field Secrets
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2768
Authors: Harliv Singh
Summary: We analyze the public values generated by a pairing-based multi-secret sharing construction in which each secret is added to a power of a common pairing value. The secrets lie in the prime subfield of the extension field containing the public values. We show that the first two public values determine the common mask whenever an explicit nonzero condition holds. We also show that the exceptional case is resolved for the parameter set considered in the numerical example. Consequently, the complete public transcript determines every secret, without requiring a participant share or an initially compromised secret. We further describe two related forms of leakage: recovery of all secrets after disclosure of one suitable secret, and a reduction in the possible values of a secret from a single public value. Our conclusions concern the field-valued, common-base masking construction analyzed here; they do not imply that pairing-based secret sharing in general is insecure.

item.title: BASTION: Lock-Step, Staggered and Sequential Share Schedules for a First-Order Masked ML-KEM NTT on FPGA
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2765
Authors: Marcos Lázaro Díaz
Summary: The Number Theoretic Transform (NTT) is the arithmetic core of ML-KEM (FIPS 203) and a prominent side-channel target in hardware. Because the transform is linear, first-order arithmetic masking applies share-wise without fresh randomness, which leaves one design decision open: when each share is processed. Published designs process the shares in sequence on one datapath, or on one datapath per share started a configurable delay apart and in random order; running both datapaths in lock-step is the third option. We implement the three schedules on one first-order masked NTT core for ML-KEM on Artix-7 and measure their cost and pre-silicon leakage under one synthesis flow. An iso-architectural unmasked control separates the cost of masking from that of parallelisation: the delivered lock-step core costs 1.56x the LUTs, 2.33x the slices and twice the DSPs of the control at an unchanged cycle count and 196.1 instead of 227.3 MHz, while the sequential core needs 9 LUTs more than the control at twice the cycles. We state when a set of samples combines both shares of a secret, measure the criterion on the RTL and use it as a cycle-accurate oracle. On a whole-design toggle model that sums both share domains, calibrated with injected flaws detected within 750 traces, no schedule leaks at first order in five pairs of runs of 10^5 traces. At second order the schedules form a scale: the lock-step core leaks in single samples, the sequential core only at the pair of samples that its public offset relates, and the staggered core in both ways at every delay we tested short of one transform. Every detected sample lies in the support view of the oracle, which flags up to 80% of the samples of a window for the univariate test, and some lie outside its form view, so lazy reduction matters. A check on the routed netlist finds no cell shared by the domains of the lock-step and staggered cores, and finds the cells that synthesis shares once the preservation attributes are removed. Silicon validation is left to future work.

item.title: Trapdoors Beyond Inversion: Recoverable Information in Public-Key Cryptography
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2764
Authors: Kanad Chakravarti, Shreyas Gupta, Bhavana Kanukurthi, Girisha Shankar
Summary: Classical trapdoor functions recover complete preimages, whereas public-key decryption needs only designated information about an encryption input. We study this distinction through trapdoor hardcore functions (TDHFs), whose trapdoor recovers a prescribed value $h(x)$ from a public evaluation $f (x)$, while $h(x)$ remains pseudorandom given the public key and evaluation. For perfectly correct primitives, we show that adaptive TDHFs characterize IND-CCA2-secure public-key encryption. The constructive direction requires only a single recoverable bit and allows noninjective public evaluations. Extending the rejection-sampling approach, we show that adaptive pseudorandomness itself controls queries to unselected candidate evaluations, without requiring full inversion. We also prove that lossy TDHFs characterize lossy public-key encryption, identifying statistical hiding of the designated recovered value as the relevant lossiness requirement. Fiber samplability together with fiber hiding yields a parameter-preserving correspondence with lossy encryption and, through the known long-message transformation, almost-always lossy trapdoor functions when the recovered-value length exceeds the fiber-sampling randomness length. Ordinary TDHFs provide the corresponding characterization of IND-CPA encryption. Together, these results make explicit the roles of adaptive recovery, conditional sampling, and randomness costs in transformations between public-key encryption and full-inversion primitives.

item.title: On Key Recovery from Exposed Neural XOR Activations in DES and TDES
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2763
Authors: Kwangjo Kim
Summary: We study the security of natural ReLU realizations of the Data Encryption Standard (DES) and two-key Triple DES (TDES) when an adversary can submit non-binary inputs and observe selected intermediate neural values. The attack exploits the piecewise-linear extension of XOR: paired inputs that differ in one expanded right-half bit reveal the corresponding round-key bit from the change in a natural XOR node. For DES, the resulting 48-bit first-round subkey leaves only the eight key-schedule bits omitted by PC-2; enumerating these bits and checking an intermediate value recovers the 56-bit effective master key. For two-key EDE TDES, the same technique recovers the first encryption subkey of K_1 and the last DES subkey used by the middle decryption under K_2; two independent 2^8 completions then recover the full 112-bit key pair. The exposed round subkey is recovered with a constant number of leakage observations per bit, giving query complexity linear in the targeted subkey length; the remaining searches are fixed-size for DES. Python experiments report exact recovery for 1,000 random DES keys and 1,000 random two-key TDES key pairs. These results concern a synthetic intermediate-oracle model for natural neural implementations and do not claim a physical attack on conventional DES/TDES hardware or software.

item.title: AirBB: Lightweight Threshold Anonymous Credentials without Random Oracles from BB Signatures
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2762
Authors: Sebastian Faust, Jonas Hofmann, Philipp-Florens Lehwalder, Hussien Othmann
Summary: Anonymous credentials are a well-studied cryptographic primitive enabling users to prove statements about their identity and selectively present personal information in an unlinkable manner. The issuer, however, is often a single point of failure. Threshold issuance addresses this by distributing the issuer across several parties such that a quorum of them must cooperate to issue credentials. Numerous constructions of single-issuer and threshold issuance anonymous credentials have been proposed. However, existing schemes each have at least one of the following weaknesses: (1) their presentations depend on the number of attributes, (2) they are not concretely efficient, or (3) they rely on the random oracle model (ROM) for non-interactive presentations.
In this work, we present a new construction of threshold anonymous credentials that has a constant presentation size of 240 bytes, rivals the efficiency of BBS, and does not rely on the random oracle model. We achieve this by combining techniques from set commitments with Boneh-Boyen (BB) signatures (Eurocrypt'04) and prove our scheme's security in the algebraic group model. This is on par with the tight security proofs of existing schemes, which typically rely on the AGM or GGM, or on assumptions justified in those models. Since signing uses linear operations, the scheme is easily thresholdizable, without requiring interaction between the issuers or preprocessing.

item.title: Superlattice methods for the shortest vector problem and discrete Gaussian sampling
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2761
Authors: Minki Hhan, Jiseung Kim, Sunyeop Kim, Thijs Laarhoven
Summary: We give worst-case algorithms for the shortest vector problem (SVP) and discrete Gaussian sampling (DGS) at arbitrary widths. Both algorithms generate lists on a dense superlattice and combine vectors along a chain down to the input lattice. Random shifts let us control the expected number of representations of a vector regardless of the lattice. For SVP we balance these counts with a novel midpoint-shell test to ensure output distributions are sufficiently uniform. For DGS we use Gaussian weights and correct the probabilities of selecting entries from the final list.
For SVP, our optimized algorithm runs in time $2^{0.409 n+o(n)}$ and space $2^{0.259 n+o(n)}$, improving the best $2^{n/2 + o(n)}$ worst-case SVP complexities of Hhan [ePrint, 2026]. For Haar-random lattices, or assuming a natural upper bound on the kissing constant, the costs of the algorithm match the $2^{0.292 n+o(n)}$ time and $2^{0.208 n+o(n)}$ space of Becker-Ducas-Gama-Laarhoven [SODA 2016].
For quantum SVP, through a series of refinements and generalizations we obtain worst-case time and space $2^{0.247n+o(n)}$. This improves the best known heuristic quantum SVP time complexity of $2^{0.256n+o(n)}$ due to Bonnetain-Chailloux-Schrottenloher-Shen [Eurocrypt 2023], without requiring any heuristic assumptions.
For discrete Gaussian sampling, we provide a sampling algorithm at any width with distribution error $2^{-\kappa}$, running in worst-case time $2^{0.292 n+o(n)} \operatorname{poly}(\kappa)$ and space $2^{0.208 n+o(n)} \operatorname{poly}(\kappa)$, improving upon the previous best $2^{n + o(n)}$ cost for sampling at arbitrary widths of Aggarwal-Dadush-Regev-Stephens-Davidowitz [STOC 2015].
As further applications, we obtain fast algorithms for approximate-SVP/CVP, bounded distance decoding, and estimating the Gaussian mass and smoothing parameter of any lattice.

item.title: Syndrome Decoding out of the Head: Structure-Aided Side-Channel Witness Recovery on SDitH
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2760
Authors: Jaeyeon Lee, Jaeho Jeon, Young-Sik Kim
Summary: Regular syndrome decoding (RSD) underlies several code-based signature schemes, including SD-in-the-Head (SDitH). Its secret witness has exactly one nonzero coordinate per block, and the selected positions must satisfy a public syndrome equation. In this work, we show how these structural constraints can be exploited to recover the complete witness from imperfect side-channel information.
We present a profiled power analysis of the witness-embedding operation in the SDitH Round-3 reference implementation. We train convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to classify the mux digits encoding each regular block and use their outputs to rank candidate positions. To correct errors in these predictions, we combine the resulting rankings with the public syndrome and the regularity constraints. We formulate this recovery problem as an affine correction system with block-validity constraints and analyze its rank, consistency, and uniqueness for the systematic parity-check matrix used in SDitH. Based on this analysis, we develop a quotient-syndrome decoder that identifies blocks whose true positions fall outside the initial candidate lists, avoiding exhaustive enumeration of block subsets.
We evaluate our attack on an ARM Cortex-M4 using measured power traces. With a single target trace per key, our approach recovers all 100 test witnesses under -Os using 4,000 profiling traces, and 91 out of 100 under -O3 using 16,000 profiling traces. Each successful recovery matches all 616 serialized witness bits. These results demonstrate how the regular structure of RSD and the public syndrome can compensate for imperfect side-channel predictions, thereby enabling full-witness recovery.

item.title: Differentially Oblivious Graph Ball Queries
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2759
Authors: Zimai Guo, Cheng Hong, Zhechen Li
Summary: A graph ball query returns all vertices within distance $r$ of a source vertex. On $N$-vertex graphs with maximum degree at most $\Delta$, ordinary breadth-first search answers such queries with $O_{\Delta,r}(1)$ record accesses. These accesses depend on private edges and can reveal graph structure. Full obliviousness hides this dependence, but incurs substantial overhead. Differential obliviousness (DO) [Chan et al., SODA'2019] trades off between privacy and efficiency by relaxing full obliviousness to $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-differential privacy on the access traces of neighboring graphs.
We study DO graph ball queries under three widely-adopted edge-level neighboring relations: add/delete, replacement, and $2$-switch. Starting from padded adjacency records, we charge all observable accesses, including preprocessing. For fixed $\Delta,r\ge2$, error probability $0<\beta<1/2$, and $0\le\delta\le(1-2\beta)/2$, we prove an $\Omega_{\Delta,r,\beta}(1+Ne^{-\varepsilon})$ expected lower bound at every sufficiently large connected graph and every public source. For every fixed $r\ge2$, we give $(\varepsilon,0)$-DO sampling algorithms with expected cost $O_{\Delta,r,\beta}(1+Ne^{-\varepsilon/C})$ using constant size of hidden workspace, where $C$ depends only on $\Delta,r$ and the neighboring relation. Especially, for $r=2$, we have $C=1$, which indicates that the algorithm achieves the tight bound under all three relations. Finally, we consider repeated queries on the same graph, where the cost of protected preprocessing can be amortized across queries. For fixed $\Delta,r,\beta$, we construct a linear-size reusable index with $(\varepsilon,0)$-DO preprocessing and constant query cost. The expected preprocessing cost is linear in $N$ when $\varepsilon$ exceeds a sufficiently large constant multiple of $\log N$.

item.title: Fine-Grained Proof Complexity for Elementary Arithmetic in Extended Frege
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2758
Authors: Andrew Krapivin, Jiatu Li, Elaine Shi
Summary: Proof complexity has historically focused on qualitative results, such as whether natural mathematical statements (e.g. the Pigeonhole Principle) admit polynomial-size proofs in certain proof systems (e.g. Resolution or Frege). In contrast to the rich theory of algorithm design, there is little understanding of how to design quantitatively efficient proofs. We initiate the study of fine-grained propositional proof complexity. Our motivation comes from an emerging line of cryptographic constructions such as the elegant work of Jain and Jin (2022), in which the efficiency of the resulting scheme is governed by the size of the underlying Extended Frege proofs.
Our main result is that the basic laws of integer arithmetic —commutativity and associativity of addition and of multiplication, together with distributivity — admit Extended Frege proofs of quasi-linear size, when addition is implemented by the schoolbook algorithm and multiplication by an FFT-based algorithm. This seemingly elementary result turns out to be surprisingly non-trivial: the natural paper-and- pencil arguments for distributivity and for associativity of multiplication translate into Extended Frege proofs of quadratic size. To reach quasi-linear size, we develop a technique we call index generalization, which we believe will find wide application in the design of efficient propositional proofs.

item.title: Affine Advantage in Guess-type Attacks on Goldreich’s PRGs: Generalization, Characterization and Countermeasures
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2757
Authors: Ximing Fu, Mo LI, Shihan Lyu
Summary: The recent guess-type attack (Eurocrypt'26) on Goldreich's pseudorandom generators exploits the strong bias toward constants that can arise when some inputs of majority-based predicates are fixed. This attack has demonstrated substantial effectiveness against several concrete parameter instances (Eurocrypt'24\&'25, Asiacrypt'24). In this paper, we generalize this attack paradigm to arbitrary affine approximations, characterize its capabilities, and develop a new predicate as a countermeasure.
We introduce a guess-and-affine-approximation (GAA) attack framework that generalizes existing guess-type attacks from constant approximations to arbitrary affine approximations of residual nonlinear predicates. To characterize the capacity of GAA attack, we introduce the bit-fixing affine advantage $\operatorname{adv}_{b'}(M_b)$, defined as the maximum affine advantage of a $b$-ary nonlinear predicate $M_b$ over all residuals with $b'$ unfixed inputs. For polynomial stretch $m=n^s$ and logarithmic nonlinear arity $b=\gamma\log_2 n$, we obtain the optimal attack complexities $C^\star$ linking bit-fixing affine advantages: (1) $C^\star>2^{cn}$ for every $c<2^{-(s-1)/\gamma}$ iff $\operatorname{adv}_{\theta b}(M_b)\to 0$ for every constant $\theta\in(0,1]$; (2) $C^\star=2^{o(n)}$ iff fixing only $o(b)$ predicate inputs can yield a residual with affine advantage $\frac{1}{2}-o(1)$, and the sufficient direction also holds for $b=\Omega(\log n)$. In particular, if $\operatorname{adv}_{b-r}(M_b) =\frac12- O\left(\frac{\log n}{n}\right)$ for $r\le s-1$, then $C^\star$ can further decrease to $n^{O(1)}$. These results complement prior analyses for arities $O(1)$, $\omega(1)\cap O(\log n)$, and $\Omega(n^{1/s})$.
Guided by the results above, we introduce the $\XOR_a$--$\MODtwelve_b$ family as a predicate candidate. We prove that every $b'$-input residual of its nonlinear component retains algebraic degree and algebraic immunity $\Theta(b')$, matching the asymptotic orders of $\MAJ$ (STOC'16). Moreover, its bit-fixing affine advantage is at most $2^{-\Omega(b')}$, whereas $\operatorname{adv}_{\theta b}(\MAJ_b)\approx \frac12$ for every fixed $\theta\in(0,1)$. Analysis shows that, for $n=1024$, $m=n^2$, and $b=54$, $\XOR$--$\MODtwelve$ can achieve $\log C^\star \approx 737$, while $\XOR$--$\MAJ$ and $\XOR$--$\MODthree$ have cost exponents of only $182$ and $599$, respectively, under the specified attack. Furthermore, our experiments show that $\MODtwelve$ offers stronger resistance to belief-propagation-based attacks.

item.title: Refined Bounds for the Smoothing Parameter of Lattices
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2756
Authors: Shanxiang Lyu
Summary: The smoothing parameter $\eta_\varepsilon(\Lambda)$ is a fundamental invariant in lattice-based cryptography. Zheng, Zhao, and Xu (AAECC 2021) proved $\eta_\varepsilon(\mathbb{Z}) \le \sqrt{\ln(\frac{2}{\varepsilon} + \frac{\varepsilon}{44})/\pi}$ and $\eta_\varepsilon(\Lambda) \le \sqrt{\ln(n - 1 + \frac{2n}{\varepsilon})/\pi}\,\mathrm{bl}(\Lambda)$. Guo, Liu, Wang, and Tian (PLOS One 2025) proposed $\eta_\varepsilon(\mathbb{Z}) \le \sqrt{\ln(\frac{2}{\varepsilon} + \frac{\varepsilon}{m})/\pi}$ for $0 < \varepsilon \le \frac{4}{m} - \frac{172}{m^6}$ ($m \ge 3$) and $\eta_\varepsilon(\Lambda) \le \sqrt{\ln((n - 1)(1 + \frac{2}{\varepsilon}))/\pi}\,\mathrm{bl}(\Lambda)$ under $\sqrt{\frac{24n+1}{n^2-1}} \le \varepsilon \le \sqrt{2}-1$. We establish three strictly sharper bounds that uniformly dominate both while removing the artificial lower bound on $\varepsilon$. First, for $0 < \varepsilon \le \rho(\mathbb{Z})-1 \approx 0.086435$, \[ \sqrt{\frac{\ln\!\left(\frac{2}{\varepsilon} + \frac{\varepsilon^2}{4} - \frac{3\varepsilon^5}{32}\right)}{\pi}} < \eta_\varepsilon(\mathbb{Z}) \le \sqrt{\frac{\ln\!\left(\frac{2}{\varepsilon} + \frac{\varepsilon^2}{4}\right)}{\pi}}; \] since Guo et al.'s condition forces $\frac{\varepsilon}{m} > \frac{\varepsilon^2}{4}$, our bound is strictly tighter for all admissible $(\varepsilon, m)$, improving the worst-case gap from $O(\varepsilon^2)$ to $O(\varepsilon^6)$. Second, for all $n \ge 2$ and $0 < \varepsilon < \min\{1, (\rho(\mathbb{Z})-1)n\}$, \[ \eta_\varepsilon(\Lambda) \le \sqrt{\frac{\ln\!\left(\frac{2}{\delta_n} + \frac{\delta_n^2}{4}\right)}{\pi}}\,\mathrm{bl}(\Lambda) < \sqrt{\frac{\ln\!\left(\frac{2n}{\varepsilon} + (n - 1) - \frac{(n^2 - 1)\varepsilon}{6n(1 + \varepsilon)}\right)}{\pi}}\,\mathrm{bl}(\Lambda), \] where $\delta_n = (1+\varepsilon)^{1/n} - 1$; the rational bound is strictly tighter than Guo et al.'s across $100\%$ of their validity window, while remaining valid as $\varepsilon \to 0^+$. Third, for any basis $\mathbf{B}$ with Gram--Schmidt vectors $\mathbf{b}_i^*$ and $M = \max_i \|\mathbf{b}_i^*\|$, define $N_\varepsilon(\mathbf{B}) = \sum_{i=1}^n (\varepsilon/2)^{M^2/\|\mathbf{b}_i^*\|^2 - 1} \in [1, n]$; then \[ \eta_\varepsilon(\Lambda) \le \sqrt{\ln\!\left(\frac{2}{\delta_{\mathrm{eff}}} + \frac{\delta_{\mathrm{eff}}^2}{4}\right)/\pi}\,M, \] where $\delta_{\mathrm{eff}} = \frac{n}{N_\varepsilon(\mathbf{B})}((1+\varepsilon)^{1/n}-1)$. For reduced bases with geometrically decaying Gram--Schmidt lengths, $N_\varepsilon(\mathbf{B}) = O(1)$ is independent of $n$, eliminating the $O(n)$ factor inside the logarithm.

item.title: Blockchain-Anchored Proactive Refresh for Dynamic Threshold Services
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2755
Authors: Seunghyun Cho, Jaeyeon Lee, Myeongjun Kim, Hyunseok Jeong, Young-Sik Kim
Summary: A long-lived threshold service must issue shares to participants that join after deployment, refresh them against a mobile adversary, and allow participants offline during a refresh to recover missed updates. We show that charging exposure solely to committed epochs is fundamentally insufficient: an aborted refresh attempt that publishes candidate update tokens can reveal the secret even if no committed epoch exceeds its corruption budget. To eliminate this exposure leakage, we index security by fine-grained states covering both committed epochs and aborted attempts. Each state's budget bounds all participants whose local material or public update records originate from that state, enforced via an append-only, durable release ledger that is never rolled back upon abort. A fixed dealer committee anchors encrypted update records in blockchain blob storage, enabling non-interactive recovery for offline participants without contacting dealers, while an interactive bisection dispute protocol deterministically attributes faulty records on chain. Our core cryptographic result is an explicit distribution-preserving shift of the actual generation transcript, establishing proactive secrecy and past-share unforgeability after dealer-state disclosure without idealizing the underlying subprotocols. An end-to-end Rust implementation benchmarks complete lifecycles across up to 1,280 participants on an EVM chain, demonstrating sub-second group recovery and practical gas costs.

item.title: A note on zero-knowledge ring switching
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2754
Authors: Andrei Kochergin
Summary: We make the ring-switching technique of Diamond and Posen zero knowledge, resolving a problem left open in the literature. Over $\mathbb{F}_{2^n}$, our technique uses $n-1$ auxiliary masks and $n-1$ quadratic constraints, checked in zero knowledge by the underlying commitment scheme.

item.title: Correlation Power Analysis on SHA-2-Based SLH-DSA
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2753
Authors: Jinwook Chang, Minjeong Lee, JIN YONG MIN, Dong-Guk Han
Summary: The stateless hash-based digital signature algorithm (SLH-DSA) repeatedly processes a fixed secret seed with varying public addresses. This paper presents non-profiled correlation power analysis of the address-based pseudorandom function for all six SHA-2 parameter sets, using separate recovery paths through SHA-256 compression rounds and message-schedule expansion. The procedures account for the input layout in which a 22-byte compressed address precedes the secret seed. For the 256-bit sets, a two-stage joint procedure recovers two 16-bit secret portions. We evaluate an STM32F303 ARM Cortex-M4 implementation using 30 secret seeds and 5,000 measured power traces per seed for each evaluated condition. Each recovery stage is evaluated with the required preceding secret values supplied correctly; the reported rates are therefore conditional stage-wise results, not end-to-end seed recovery rates. Compression-round stages achieve 100% success under both forest-of-random-subsets and Winternitz one-time-signature-plus address conditions. Under forest-of-random-subsets addresses, all message-schedule stages achieve 100% success for the 128- and 192-bit sets. For both 256-bit variants, joint recovery achieves 100%, whereas recovery of message word $W_{12}$ achieves 66.7%; recovery of $W_7$ achieves 70.0% and 80.0% for the fast and small variants, respectively. An alternative first stage is also provided for 128-bit Winternitz one-time-signature-plus addresses. These results show that side-channel protection must cover both compression rounds and message-schedule expansion.

item.title: An efficient Failure Probability Estimator for LWE-based encryption, and application to IBE
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2751
Authors: Julien CAM
Summary: In recent years, lattice-based cryptography has proven to be a source of post-quantum cryptosystems. In particular, the blueprint of Learning With Errors (LWE) encryption enabled the creation of Kyber, chosen by NIST to be standardized as ML-KEM. Because of the structure of LWE encryption, the decryption of a ciphertext can give an incorrect plaintext. This event (a decryption failure) happens randomly with some probability. Since this is a problem for both functionality and security, we must ensure that this failure probability is cryptographically negligible. Usually, this is assessed with theoretical approximations and upper-bounds. The authors of Kyber used a Python program to compute that probability more precisely, enabling to fine-tune the compression of the ciphertext, hence reducing its size. However, because of its performances, this program has been limited to Kyber, and all the other schemes are still studied theoretically. In this paper, we design a more efficient Failure Probability Estimator, that we implement in low-level languages (C and CUDA C++), to reach higher parameters used in real schemes based on structured LWE. We illustrate some benefits of our tool with two Identity-Based Encryption schemes. For the first scheme, our tool allows to reduce the size of the ciphertext by about 20%. For the second one, we reduce the failure probability (thus improving security) without impacting the scheme (key size, ciphertext size, etc.).

item.title: Information Loss Is All You Need: TC⁰ Pseudorandomness from Worst-Case Lattices
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2752
Authors: Chen Qian
Summary: Pseudorandomness plays a central role in algorithms, complexity theory, and cryptography. We ask whether deterministic information loss alone can yield post-quantum pseudorandomness with $\mathrm{TC}^0$ evaluation. Learning with errors (LWE) hides linear measurements with random noise. Learning with rounding (LWR) replaces noise with deterministic rounding, but a standard polynomial-modulus hardness reduction requires parameters tailored to a predetermined sample bound. Decisional Diffie–Hellman offers a noiseless algebraic route to pseudorandomness, but its standard instantiations are vulnerable to quantum algorithms. We show that deterministic rounding achieves this under quantum worst-case lattice hardness, with fixed polynomial parameters and no predetermined sample bound.
We introduce the learning with algebraic rounding (LAR) assumption, which applies an explicit integer rounding map to blocks of secret-dependent linear measurements and encodes the result in a lattice quotient. For one fixed family with polynomially bounded modulus and dimensions, its deterministic labels on exactly uniform, secret-independent public matrices are computationally indistinguishable from independent uniform labels for every polynomial number of classical random examples. Our classical reduction from Gaussian LWE, combined with the quantum worst-case reduction to LWE, bases LAR on GapSVP and SIVP over general lattices at approximation factor $\widetilde{O}(q)$, where $q$ is the modulus.
To prove this, we develop a source-independent affine transport framework that may be of independent interest. Using public affine maps sampled independently of the hidden errors, it transports the Gaussian error law close to uniform on the rounding map’s zero-label fiber while preserving exactly uniform public matrices. For every fixed inverse-polynomial accuracy, we give a polynomial-time sampler for the same public parameter family.
This yields the first post-quantum weak pseudorandom function with joint key-and-input evaluation in $\mathrm{TC}^0$, secure against uniform quantum polynomial-time distinguishers given any polynomial number of classical uniform random examples. We also establish the hardness of learning polynomial-size two-hidden-layer ReLU networks from noiseless uniform random examples, even for quantum polynomial-time improper learners.

item.title: Practical Optimal Bucket Sets with Power-of-Two Radices for LFG-Based MSM Algorithms
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2750
Authors: Guiwen Luo
Summary: Fixed point multi-scalar multiplication (MSM) is a major computational component of pairing-based SNARK proof generation. The Luo--Fu--Gong (LFG) framework is a variant of Pippenger's bucket method that uses a multiplier set $M$ and precomputed point multiples to reduce the number of buckets and online point additions. For radix $q$ and a positive multiplier set $M$, covering all digit residues requires a bucket set of size at least $q/(2|M|)$. Previous constructions approaching this bound based on primitive roots or power-residue classes impose radix restrictions that exclude $q=2^c$, thereby requiring additional binary-to-radix conversion in software implementations.
We present two main bucket set constructions for power-of-two radices $q=2^c$, using the multiplier sets $M=\{1,2,3\}$ and $M=\{1,3\}$, respectively. Their cardinalities are $q/6+O(\log q)$ and $q/4+2$, respectively, so both asymptotically attain the counting bound $q/(2|M|)$ while allowing efficient radix-digit extraction through shifts and masks.
We further give two generalizations. Using consecutive powers of $3$ as multipliers yields bucket sets of size $q/(2\ell)+O(\log q)$ for every fixed positive integer $\ell$. For $\ell=2^d$ and $c\ge d+2$, consecutive odd multipliers yield bucket sets of size $q/(2\ell)+d+1$.
We also present scalar conversion and two strategies for handling the leading digit, allowing the bucket set constructions to be used within the LFG framework.

item.title: Shielded Bitcoin: Private Transfers on the Bitcoin L1
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2749
Authors: Clara Shikhelman, Mikhail Komarov, Aleksei Moskvin
Summary: This paper introduces Shielded Bitcoin, a protocol for private transfer of Bitcoin directly on the Bitcoin L1, requiring no changes to Bitcoin consensus. Its design borrows from the architecture of Zcash and earlier shielded-note systems: value is held as encrypted notes, spends are marked by public nullifiers, and validity is established by zero-knowledge proofs. Unlike Zcash, Shielded Bitcoin introduces no dedicated consensus chain: all protocol data is published on Bitcoin, transfer validity is enforced through PIPEs v2 [ACG+26], and shielded state is reconstructed by deterministic replay of accepted transfers in Bitcoin order. At the metaprotocol transfer level, Shielded Bitcoin is non-custodial: spending authority remains with user-controlled wallet keys encrypted in a ciphertext, and neither indexers nor the replay layer receive authority to spend user notes.
A shielded transfer does not publicly reveal its amount, sender, receiver, and place in the transfer graph, while keeping the validity of every encrypted state transition publicly verifiable. Shielded state, comprising the note tree, nullifier set, and block-level root history, is maintained entirely off-chain: any two correct implementations replaying the same Bitcoin history derive identical protocol state without coordination. The paper defines the transfer model, note structure, ciphertext-derived note leaves, nullifier rules, transaction binding, replay semantics, and publication assumptions. Peg-in and peg-out, the mechanisms by which value enters and exits the shielded transfer system, belong to the broader system and fall outside the scope of this paper.

item.title: TFNP in the Random Oracle Model
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2748
Authors: Noah Fleming, Mika Göös, Ziyi Guan, Oliver Korten, Daniel Mitropolsky, Toniann Pitassi, Artur Riazanov, Dmitry Sokolov, Tianqi Yang, Weiqiang Yuan
Summary: We determine which major TFNP classes are hard in the random oracle model (ROM). Prior work establishes average-case hardness of highly structured subclasses of TFNP from strong cryptographic assumptions such as LWE and indistinguishability obfuscation. It is not known whether weaker assumptions such as one-way functions imply hardness of any of the standard TFNP subclasses, even in the worst case. The ROM, where all parties have query access to a random function, lies, morally, between these two regimes: a random function is one-way, but public-key cryptography cannot be built from it in a black-box way. We refer to this setting as \emph{Romantica}.
Our first result settles a long-standing open problem: PPAD, the class of total search problems reducible to finding a Nash equilibrium, is hard on average in Romantica. Combined with the known hardness of PLS (local search), this gives average-case hardness of EoPL = PPAD \cap PLS. In contrast, we show that UEoPL can be solved in Romantica with polynomially many oracle queries by a computationally unbounded solver, a sharp distinction between EoPL and UEoPL. This resolves the black-box hardness landscape of all major TFNP classes in Romantica.
Finally, we initiate the study of separations between TFNP subclasses in Romantica: PWPP and PPA do not reduce to PLS under \emph{public-coin} reductions.

item.title: MODDIV-WC: Unit-Anchored Toeplitz/Hankel Rounding with Exact Binary-LWE Masking and an IND-CCA Security Route
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2747
Authors: Samir Bouftass
Summary: \begin{abstract} We present MODDIV-WC, a public-key encryption and key-encapsulation candidate based on a widened Hankel linear map followed by deterministic integer division, together with an implicit-rejection Fujisaki--Okamoto wrapper, MODDIV-WC-FO. The construction uses a secret vector whose first coordinate is fixed to one and whose remaining coordinates are sampled from a positive interval. This unit anchor makes the Hankel map surjective for every admissible secret, a property that is central to the proof.
The security analysis has four layers. First, we give an exact embedding of binary-secret LWE into the widened Hankel map using a parity mask that reproduces the MODDIV-WC secret distribution without statistical loss. Second, in an ideal public-key hybrid, a strong leftover-hash argument hides the challenge key. Third, adapting the Renyi-divergence boundary method of prior LWR and MP-LWR work, we prove a transfer lemma for the unit-anchored MODDIV-WC secret distribution. This avoids the earlier requirement that the probability of crossing a rounding boundary be negligible and instead preserves one-way success probabilities with a multiplicative Renyi loss. Fourth, we combine one-way chosen-plaintext security with the implicit-rejection modular Fujisaki--Okamoto analysis of Hofheinz, Hovelmanns, and Kiltz to derive IND-CCA security in the classical random-oracle model.
For an explicit asymptotic family, the correctness, Renyi, leftover-hash, binary-secret-LWE, and random-oracle losses are simultaneously negligible, while the source LWE noise remains inverse-polynomial. Together with classical worst-case-to-LWE reductions and the binary-secret/modulus transformations of Brakerski, Langlois, Peikert, Regev, and Stehle, this yields an internally audited candidate route from polynomial-factor worst-case lattice hardness to IND-CCA security. No practical 128-bit parameters, QROM proof, or deployment claim is made. \end{abstract}

item.title: Differential Cryptanalysis of SPEEDY: Revised Security Evaluation and Improved Key Recovery Attack
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2746
Authors: Xinwei Yu, Wentao Zhang, Zairui Zhang, Chunning Zhou
Summary: The resistance of a block cipher against differential cryptanalysis (DC) is a fundamental criterion for evaluating its security. SPEEDY is a family of low-latency SPS-type block ciphers designed by Leander et al. The designers presented two evaluations of SPEEDY against DC: the first restricted 1-bit-to-1-bit differential propagations through the S-box and used the higher-order branch numbers to estimate the maximum expected differential probability (EDP) of differential trails; the second imposed a structural restriction and assumed that all 1-bit-to-1-bit propagations through an active S-box are possible to estimate the minimum number of active S-boxes. Zhang later exhibited a counterexample to the designers' first evaluation and introduced the notion of partition branch number, relaxing some of the propagation restrictions to allow multi-bit-to-1-bit transitions on some S-box layers and refining the evaluation. However, these evaluations consider only restricted spaces of differential characteristics and therefore inaccurately estimate the security of SPEEDY against DC, which means that the resistance of SPEEDY against DC remains unclear so far. To address this problem, we propose an efficient search method based on search patterns. Unlike previous evaluations, our method imposes no a priori structural restrictions on the allowed differential characteristics; it uses computational pruning to keep the search tractable and performs a conservative security evaluation of the pruned region, thereby providing an accurate evaluation over the global space. At the framework level, we decompose an r-round differential characteristic into an (r-1)-round core trail and an r-round extended trail. By extending a core trail independently at both ends, the two additional S-box layers are handled by two separate models, each containing only one S-box layer and solvable efficiently. At the implementation level, we further introduce a short-round reuse via hash-map concatenation technique, which concatenates short-round core trails to construct longer-round core trails, thereby avoiding expensive long-round MILP models. For 4 rounds, we narrow the minimum number of active S-boxes from the previously reported 35 to [33,34] and find a characteristic with 34 active S-boxes outside the previous search spaces. We also obtain the highest-probability differential characteristics known to date for 2 to 5 rounds. In particular, the 2-, 3-, and 4-round characteristics disprove the designers' branch-number-based security claims. Furthermore, using the quasidifferential framework, we evaluate the found characteristics and obtain several 5-round distinguishers outperforming those used in existing key recovery attacks in terms of EDP. Finally, we optimize the probabilistic extension parameters used in a previous key recovery attack, which yields the best known key recovery attack on SPEEDY-7-192, with data complexity $2^{173.48}$ and time complexity $2^{173.69}$ encryptions.

item.title: The Price of Agreement in Secure Multiparty Computation
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2745
Authors: Ran Cohen, Pouyan Forghani, Juan Garay, Vassilis Zikas
Summary: Secure multi-party computation (MPC) cannot guarantee output delivery, in general, in the dishonest-majority setting. Security of MPC is therefore relaxed to security with abort, where the adversary may prevent honest parties from obtaining their output. The standard notion of \emph{unanimous abort} (UA-MPC) ensures that either all honest parties obtain their output or all of them abort. Goldwasser and Lindell [JCRYPT '05] introduced the relaxed notion of \emph{selective abort}, allowing some honest parties to abort and others to obtain their output. While two-round SA-MPC can be achieved over point-to-point channels, two-round UA-MPC necessitates the second round to be over broadcast. The price of agreement in dishonest-majority MPC is thus tied to the round complexity of broadcast with unanimous abort (UA-broadcast).
The round complexity of broadcast has been extensively studied for more than four decades. Garay, Katz, Koo, and Ostrovsky [FOCS '07] (GKKO) proved that the expected round complexity of broadcast protocols tolerating $t$ corruptions is at least $2n/(n-t)-1$. Their argument, however, relies on all honest parties obtaining an honest sender's input, and does not extend to UA-broadcast. Recently, Cohen {\em et al.} [TCC '26] showed that UA-MPC is possible in an expected constant number of rounds when a constant fraction of the parties is honest, and asked whether this extends to $n-o(n)$ corruptions.
In this work we answer this question in the negative: Agreement alone already incurs the GKKO barrier. Concretely, we prove that for $t\leq n-2$, UA-broadcast---and hence UA-MPC---requires at least $t/(2(n-t))$ rounds in expectation, matching the asymptotic bound for broadcast without abort. As a corollary, expected-constant-round UA-MPC is possible if and only if a constant fraction of the parties is honest.
Next, we consider UA-broadcast protocols that terminate in an {\em a-priori} known round, and show that the bound that the argument of GKKO gives for broadcast holds for them exactly. Combined with the broadcast protocol of Dolev and Strong [SICOMP '83], our bound is tight for arbitrarily many corruptions.

item.title: Phantom Timing Leaks on Cortex-M4: A Pre-registered Evaluation of ML-KEM Decapsulation
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2744
Authors: Amadou Tidiane Anne
Summary: Fixed-versus-random timing tests in the style of dudect are a cheap first check of constant-time behaviour, and on microcontrollers the cycle counter makes them exact to the cycle. We report a pre-registered evaluation of ML-KEM decapsulation on an STM32F411 (Cortex-M4) covering nine implementations of PQM4 (clean, m4fspeed, m4fstack for ML-KEM-512/768/1024) and a positive control in which we restored the pre-KyberSlash division formulas. Each of the 44 campaigns used in the analysis has 100,000 trials and checks every result. With invalid ciphertexts (random bytes, or one modified byte), no difference is detected in 18 of 18 campaigns, and both classes always have exactly the same cycle count, while the control is detected every time (|t| up to 1,877). With fresh valid ciphertexts, however, all nine implementations are flagged, with differences of 4 to 15 cycles and |t| >= 19,000 (or infinite, when both classes have zero variance). A matched control, in which both classes run the same code before the measured call, removes the difference for seven of the nine. An A/A test, in which both classes decapsulate the same bytes, still yields |t| = 12,864 for one implementation. Deterministic few-cycle differences can therefore come from the measurement harness alone: on a part with flash wait states, an instruction cache and prefetching, they can appear when the code around the measured call changes. We also show that per-trial correctness checks matter: they exposed a functional bug in PQM4's ML-KEM-1024 m4fstack (220 wrong shared secrets out of 49,830), which upstream had fixed shortly before. We report every deviation from the pre-registration, including a build error of our own, and publish data, binaries and code (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23921418).

item.title: Challenge Binding in FRESCO SPDZ2k: A Message-Level Case Study
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2743
Authors: Mingzhao Huang
Summary: FRESCO's SPDZ2k suite derives its batched MAC-check coefficients from a setup-time public seed, making the stream predictable before opening shares are sent. We examine this implementation path at a pinned revision. A source-level derivation accounts for low-limb carries and high-bit corrections and shows that the value-share shifts $e=(r_j,-r_i)$ preserve the check residual while retaining the original MAC shares. A message-level harness executes this deviation against unmodified honest opening code. The recorded sum/product outputs violate a relation required for every possible input of the corrupt party, and the test framework records normal completion. The retained evidence includes two-, three-, and four-party executions with dummy preprocessing. The predictable-seed attack template appears in Rushing at SPDZ, and FRESCO's issue tracker recorded the per-check randomness requirement in 2018; our contribution is the SPDZ2k public-seed path, its explicit kernel witness, and the implementation evidence. We also give a conditional single-opening analysis and assess a four-file candidate mitigation that rejects seven recorded tampering scenarios while preserving four honest baselines. Audit tools and descriptive corpora provide context. The proof concerns the specified value-share deviation; unrestricted malicious behavior, production preprocessing, and a complete mitigation argument remain outside the established result.

item.title: Differentially $2^t$-uniform quadrinomials with high nonlinearity
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2742
Authors: Niki Spithaki, Enrico Piccione, Lilya Budaghyan, Alexander Kholosha
Summary: In this paper, we discuss some cryptographic properties of a family of quadrinomials constructed as a generalization of a known family of APN quadrinomials. In particular, we show that this family produces differentially $2^t$-uniform quadrinomials with the same Walsh spectrum as the Gold power function $x^{2^t+1}$ over $\mathbb{F}_{2^n}$. We also discuss whether this family provides permutations.

item.title: Leakage-Resilient Computation via Matrix Refreshing
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2741
Authors: Stefan Dziembowski, Sebastian Faust
Summary: Leakage-resilient cryptography protects secrets against side-channel attacks, in which a physical implementation reveals partial information about its internal state. A fundamental primitive in this area is a leakage-resilient storage, which allows a secret to be stored in a way that remains secure even if an adversary learns some information about the storage's internal state. A popular approach represents a secret as the inner product of two $n$-bit vectors, called shares. The shares are stored and processed separately by two parts of the implementation, called the left and right parties. Because leakage accumulates over time, the shares must be refreshed repeatedly. We prove that a simple refresh, in which the left party multiplies its share by a uniform invertible matrix $M$ and the right party multiplies its share by $M^{-1}$, is secure under continual local leakage. After $T$ refreshes, each allowing at most $\lambda$ bits of leakage per party, the transcripts for two stored secrets are at statistical distance at most $C\cdot T\cdot 2^{6\lambda-n/9}$ for an absolute constant $C$.
We also obtain a Boolean-circuit compiler with statistical privacy error at most $C\cdot S\cdot 2^{18\lambda-n/27}$ for $S$ operations and at most $\lambda$ bits of local leakage per party per operation. The guarantee covers repeated stateful evaluations with adaptively chosen public inputs, with $S$ counting all operations across invocations. Thus, for polynomial-size circuits, a constant leakage fraction is tolerated with share length depending only on the security parameter. We formalize the refreshing bound, the composition and compiler guarantees, and the expected-work bounds in Lean 4. Our results also provide efficient simulation: the leakage can be reproduced from the public inputs and the circuit outputs alone, with expected polynomial overhead.

item.title: Dual Coppersmith: Finding Small Roots Without Multivariate Polynomial Systems
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2740
Authors: Taehun Kang, Jebin Kim, Changmin Lee, JeongHwan Lee
Summary: The multivariate Coppersmith algorithm is a central tool in public-key cryptanalysis for finding a small hidden root of modular polynomial equations. It consists of two stages. First, a lattice-reduction (LR) stage constructs auxiliary equations satisfied by the hidden root over $\mathbb Z$. Second, a root-recovery (RR) stage solves these equations. The RR stage can be a bottleneck: auxiliary polynomials may not isolate the root, and solving them can take exponential time in the worst case, even when LR is feasible.
We introduce Dual Coppersmith, which replaces algebraic root recovery with geometric recovery from a modular orthogonal lattice. Our construction embeds the hidden root as a short lattice vector, and we prove that LLL recovers its direction whenever a sufficient gap separates it from all independent lattice vectors. The root can then be recovered directly from coordinate ratios. To analyze this gap, we propose a heuristic model for the second successive minimum by examining both the full lattice and a structured sublattice. Under this model, Dual Coppersmith achieves the standard Coppersmith product-size bound without solving an auxiliary polynomial system. Experiments on the approximate common divisor (ACD) and Herrmann-May (HM) problems support the model's predictions and demonstrate root recovery in higher-dimensional instances where the Gröbner-based baseline reaches its timeout.

item.title: Archive Certificates for ML-DSA-87 Authorizations from an Exact Bounded Relation
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2739
Authors: Yacine Alloul
Summary: A blockchain that signs every transaction with FIPS 204 ML-DSA-87 keeps 4,627 bytes of signature per transaction forever. We describe and measure an archive certificate: one hash-based proof, for a range of already validated blocks, of knowledge of canonical FIPS 204 signatures on exactly the recorded messages under the keys resolved from chain state. Fresh blocks keep native verification. The construction starts from an exact bounded relation for ML-DSA-87 verification once the high bits $u = w_1'$ are fixed. The main certificate keeps $u$ hidden and proves the SHAKE256 challenge hash inside the proof, by a GKR argument for Keccak-f[1600] over the same WHIR commitment as the lattice relation. For 65,536 signatures we measured 104.09 bytes per signature in a Johnson-regime family, which has a classical bound only, and 126.89 in a unique-decoding family, against 4,627 bytes raw. The price is a slow prover and a verifier slower than native verification. At $2^{64}$ queries and $2^{20}$ verification submissions, conditional on cited Reed–Solomon proximity theorems, the classical random-oracle extraction error is below $2^{-188.07}$ for the Johnson family and below $2^{-201.99}$ for unique decoding. In the quantum random oracle model we state, for the unique-decoding family only, an extraction-failure bound below $2^{-129.67}$ at $2^{64}$ quantum queries; it is not a work factor. An external review is outstanding, so certificate-only bootstrap stays disabled.

item.title: Leakage-Tolerant Computation without Leakage-Free Setup
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2737
Authors: Yaohua Ma, Yifan Song
Summary: Leakage-tolerant multi-party computation (MPC) ensures that leakage from each honest party’s internal state reveals no more than the leakage from honest parties' individual inputs and outputs, beyond the standard security guarantee of MPC. Previous constructions either require a leakage-free preprocessing, or rely on indistinguishability obfuscation in the common reference string (CRS) model and only achieve semi-honest security.
In the computational setting, assuming only an augmented non-committing encryption scheme, we show that every adaptively well-formed functionality admits a semi-honest leakage-tolerant MPC protocol, without any leakage-free preprocessing execution or CRS. Under the decisional Diffie–Hellman assumption, we further extend this result to malicious security in the CRS model for all deterministic functionalities. The limitation of deterministic functions is subject to an impossibility result of leakage-based coin-tossing protocols.
In the information-theoretic setting, we show that secure erasure enables statistically secure leakage-tolerant MPC of arbitrary functionalities assuming strictly less than half of the participants are maliciously corrupted. We complement this construction with an impossibility result: without secure erasure, general-purpose statistically secure leakage-tolerant MPC with leakage-oblivious simulation, an important property to enable universal composition, is impossible in the plain model, even when all parties are honest.
As a further application, we also obtain information-theoretic leakage-tolerant circuits against bounded communication leakage, while all prior works are restricted only to the weaker variant of leakage-resilient circuits.

item.title: The Fairest of Them All: Best-of-Both-Worlds Fair Leader Election
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2738
Authors: Chen-Da Liu-Zhang, Elisaweta Masserova, Kelsey Melissaris, Lawrence Roy, Sophia Yakoubov
Summary: Fair leader election is the problem of sampling an unbiased random party out of a set of $n$ parties. The seminal impossibility result of Cleve (STOC 1986) applies to this setting, and shows that the result of the election cannot be unbiased against a dishonest majority. Recent work has achieved the weaker property of game-theoretic fairness, where behaving dishonestly cannot improve one’s chances of being elected. However, such protocols allow even a single corrupt party to bias the outcome. In this work, we introduce best-of-both-worlds (BoBW) fairness, where a small number $t_S$ of corrupt parties cannot bias the result, and even a larger number $t_{GT}$ of corrupt parties still cannot improve their collective election chances (CSP-fairness) nor hurt the election chances of any given honest party (MM-fairness). We present a protocol for BoBW fair leader election for $t_S + t_{GT} < n$. We then prove a generalization of Cleve’s impossibility, and show that this protocol is optimal. Next, in the setting of statistical security we find that BoBW fairness is uninteresting, as it is only possible for an honest majority, where we can get also unbiased leader election. Finally, in the setting of perfect security, we present a BoBW protocol achieving CSP-fairness and strong fairness for $t_S + 1 = t_{CSP} = \frac{n}{3}$, and prove that this is also optimal.

item.title: PS-BKZ: Decoupling Outer Propagation and Local Processing in BKZ by Parameter Separation
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2736
Authors: Hutao Song, Hua Guo, Yang Sun, Fengju Gao, Zongyang Zhang, Qianhong Wu
Summary: This work provides a systematic study of parameter separation in Block Korkine–Zolotarev (BKZ) reduction. We propose a general framework with separate parameters for outer propagation and the dominant local computation. The framework covers the local parameter settings of standard BKZ and variants using extended preprocessing, dimensions for free, or progressive sieving, with corresponding adaptations to the outer operations. This allows less expensive local processing without narrowing the outer propagation range.
Within this framework, we give idealized and executable constructions that use inner BKZ with a smaller blocksize to supply local vectors for larger outer blocks. We derive a worst-case quality bound for the idealized construction and analyze its quality–cost behavior using a practical fixed-point model. Experiments on the executable construction cover random q-ary bases up to dimension 300 and SVP Challenge bases up to dimension 240. The detailed comparisons at n ≥ 200 show lower mean root-Hermite factors (RHFs) and 14.1%–59.3% shorter mean running times than BKZ 2.0. Joint improvements generally become more frequent with dimension. On q-ary inputs against BKZ 2.0 with blocksize 50, their frequency increases from 15.56% at n = 150 to 73.33% at n = 300.

item.title: Perseus: A Full-Stack System for Homomorphic Model Inference
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2735
Authors: Alessandro Zirilli, Davide Marincione, Evgenios M. Kornaropoulos, Giuseppe Ateniese, Emanuele Rodolà
Summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have made it exceptionally convenient for users to send their private data to model providers, which process them in plaintext. Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) promises to secure remote inference by computing directly on encrypted data, yet it has remained prohibitively slow. The effort to make it practical remains fragmented, with most existing frameworks being closed-source, which keeps progress from compounding. We present Perseus, a free and open Python software library that supports the full stack of encrypted model inference, from the cryptographic backend and data packing, to encrypted nonlinearities and end-to-end model execution. Perseus ships with built-in novel optimizations, one at each level of the stack: in-kernel regeneration of key-switching keys at the (i) backend level, a complex variant of Cachemir packing at the (ii) data level, and a state-of-the-art bootstrap placer that is both packing- and magnitude-aware at the (iii) model level. Perseus achieves state-of-the-art latency across multiple models and modalities, within $3\%$ of the plaintext models' accuracy and perplexity. Remarkably, it is $3.96\times$ faster at single-token decoding than any other implementation on Llama-3-8B. We initiate, for the first time, a public speedrun on encrypted GPT-2, so that progress can compound.

item.title: Finite-Batch q-ary OT Extension for High-Arity Private Lookup: Certified Radix--Code Co-Design
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2734
Authors: Zhuoran Zhang
Summary: High-arity oblivious transfer is a natural abstraction for private lookup: a $\delta$-bit table address selects one entry out of $2^\delta$ candidates. This paper characterizes the finite-batch design space of the CCG q-ary OT-extension family and derives certified radix-selection rules. For $q=2^r$, we formulate radix-code selection as a security-constrained discrete optimization problem that accounts for subfield-check padding, code dimension, required distance, base-OT count, and q-ary symbol width. We derive exact communication thresholds showing when reduced base OTs can compensate for larger q-ary encoding cost. Then we convert the Griesmer bound into communication lower bounds, yielding certificates for regions where non-binary radices cannot improve communication, are provably beneficial, or remain dependent on better code constructions. Finally, we instantiate the framework with simplex and BCH constructions and CodeTables entries, and verify the selected $\delta=12$ codes with Magma.

item.title: Cryptanalysis of MinRank 2.0
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2733
Authors: Nicolas Aragon, Maxime Bros, Ray Perlner, Daniel Smith-Tone, Javier Verbel
Summary: MinRank is an NP-complete problem underlying the security of several post-quantum schemes. It is the hardness assumption of the NIST second-round signature candidate Mirath and of the encryption schemes of Chatterjee et al.\ and Debris-Alazard et al.\ at Eurocrypt 2026. Moreover, it is ubiquitous in the cryptanalysis of multivariate schemes, among them the third-round candidates UOV, MAYO, QR-UOV, and SNOVA.
In this work, we revisit the attacks on MinRank. On the combinatorial side, we improve the polynomial part of the kernel-search attack by sharing its linear algebra across guesses, which lowers its cost by 3 to 6 bits on the Mirath parameters and the Courtois challenges, and by up to 3 bits in combination with the hybrid approach. With the improved attack, we solved Courtois challenge~D, open since 2001: an instance over $\mathbb{F}_2$ with $19 \times 19$ matrices, $81$ unknowns, and target rank $10$, solved in 11434 CPU days, an estimated $2^{61}$ bit opetations. Our multi-threaded C++ code is publicly available.
On the algebraic side, we show that the complexity of the Kipnis--Shamir (KS) attack is less understood than the literature suggests: the existing estimates rely on a generic Hilbert series that does not predict the rank of the Macaulay matrices of the KS equations. We prove a lower bound on the corank that explains the discrepancy, show that the attack requires a reduced instance with $k \leq m - r$, and derive corrected complexity estimates, which are $1$ to $24$ bits above the best other attack on every Mirath parameter set. We also extend the Support-Minors and Minors modelings with the field equations, which lowers their estimates over small fields: for $q = 2$ and $m = n = 22$, by 9 to 205 bits for Support-Minors and by 17 to 278 bits for Minors. The rank predictions behind the algebraic estimates are stated as assumptions and verified experimentally.

item.title: MuCPay: Breaking the Quadratic Bottleneck in Scriptless Multi-Party Oracle-Based Conditional Payments
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2732
Authors: Yaning Wang, Na Wang, Chuan Li, Yongda Zhang, Junsong Fu
Summary: Oracle-based conditional payments triggered by real-world events support decentralized finance applications. However, dense independent bilateral deployments require $\Theta(Nn^2)$ outcome authorizations and $\Theta(n^2)$ settlement signatures for $n$ parties and $N$ outcomes. To go beyond two-party settings, we propose MuCPay, a multi-party oracle-based conditional payment protocol combining (i) $\Theta(Nn)$ off-chain signing shares with one on-chain settlement signature and (ii) BIP340-compatible scriptless settlement on Bitcoin. At its core, MuCPay introduces hash-bound adaptor multi-signatures (HB-AMS) that aggregate parties' conditional authorizations into a compact joint pre-signature. Its single-nonce structure and hash-bound adaptor integration enable efficient multi-party pre-signing. Unlike Double-Layer AMS (EuroS&P'26), HB-AMS produces a standard BIP340 signature under an aggregate public key, enabling direct Taproot key-path settlement. Under static corruption with one honest signer, we prove concurrent new-message unforgeability (CUF) and early-settlement resistance (ES) under our stated algebraic random-oracle model. For 128 parties and 16 outcomes, median complete local preparation takes 2.093 s. For protocol preparation (1.862 s for MuCPay), native-profile projections place VweTS (NDSS’23) and ParaSwap (USENIX’25) work at 1.67 × 10⁴ and 5.05 × 10⁵ times MuCPay's, respectively. Settlement uses one 64-byte signature, while the modeled independent-DLC deployment requires 281.5× as many transaction vbytes. These results demonstrate practical, scalable multi-party oracle-based conditional payments.

item.title: FixSampZ: A Fixed-Point Hardware-Efficient Discrete Gaussian Sampler for Falcon Signatures
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2731
Authors: Pushpendra Singh, Akshara K B, Utsav Banerjee, Navin Kashyap
Summary: Falcon, a NIST-standardized post-quantum signature algorithm, offers compact signatures but relies on hardware-intensive floating-point arithmetic. Building on recent theoretical fixed-point formulations, we present a completely floating-point-free hardware architecture for SamplerZ, Falcon’s primary signing bottleneck. By utilizing zero-cost hardware bit-sliced retagging of fixed-point data, which software avoids due to instruction overheads, we enforce tighter data formats at every stage boundary without area or latency penalties. Furthermore, executing floor functions as trivial two's-complement arithmetic right shifts eliminates the complex floor-prediction and redundant data-paths required by floating-point designs. Implemented on UltraScale+ FPGA, our fixed-point sampler exactly matches all 1,024 official test vectors and requires 38% fewer LUTs, 21% less FFs and 36% less DSPs compared to the floating-point baseline, with 21% fewer cycles at a higher clock frequency. We also demonstrate that substituting the baseline ChaCha20 PRNG with lightweight NIST-standardized Ascon-XOF128 achieves further 2-3 × hardware resource savings with zero sampling latency overhead.

item.title: Kaiburr: ML-KEM at (much) higher security
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2730
Authors: Swechchha Adhikari, Vadim Lyubashevsky, Peter Schwabe
Summary: With deployment of standardized post-quantum cryptography well on the way, discussions continue about concrete choices of schemes and parameter sets. For example, while NIST standardized structured-lattice-based ML-KEM, European agencies like BSI and ANSSI favor unstructured-lattice-based FrodoKEM.
