Another discussion revolves around different approaches to hybrid deployments – either combining post-quantum schemes with "traditional" elliptic-curve cryptography (or RSA) or combining multiple different post-quantum schemes. The typical question for systems engineers to ask is what the "best" or "most conservative" approach is within a certain performance budget.
In this paper we add a data point to this discussion by investigating how to scale ML-KEM to (much) higher security levels of the underlying MLWE problem. We first observe that increasing security simply by increasing the module rank $k$ quickly reaches a limit imposed by decryption failure probability. We then propose a generalization of the noise distribution, which enables scaling to much larger module rank and MLWE hardness, while preserving the essence of ML-KEM, most notably arithmetic in the ring $\mathbb{Z}_{3329}[X]/(X^{256}+1)$ and a simple and constant-time secret / noise generation.
We select three concrete parameter sets of this high-security variant of ML-KEM, which we call Kaiburr. We present benchmarking results for optimized implementations of Kaiburr on 64-bit Intel CPUs and on the Asymmetric Cryptography Coprocessor (ACC) of the Pavona open-source silicon framework. Based on these benchmarks, we argue that, for example, a hybrid of FrodoKEM-976 and Kaiburr-1792 not only offers better performance than FrodoKEM-1344, it also offers protection against a broader range of hypothetical future attacks against (M)LWE.

item.title: Quotienting Redundant Tables: Practical Master-Key Recovery from WBSLT White-Box AES
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2729
Authors: Jiseok Bang, Seungkwang Lee
Summary: Enlarging lookup-table addresses does not hide smaller selectors when the complete public table factors through a core with distinct rows and distinct columns. We demonstrate this condition in WBSLT, a white-box AES design presented at NDSS 2026 that reports resistance to several structural attacks. In the released general generator, the joint output of each group of four first-round TypeII tables has an exact 16 × 16 quotient of its 64 × 64 address space. Mapping its row and column classes to observed addresses recovers the original nibble partition of each AES input byte. Public tables implementing encoded XOR supply compatible output coordinates. Under the generator’s strictly linear input decoder, two 16-point restrictions of each keyed AES S-box then identify its embedded key byte; independent exhaustive checks confirm this property for all 256 byte keys. Using public tables and traces of chosen encoded inputs, we recover every key in 200 general instances that passed 200,000 reference AES block tests, after a median of 146 and at most 221 inputs. Separate 200-instance cohorts of the released optimized C source and its one-line functional repair also yield every key; only the repair passes the AES tests. An adjacent-round adaptation recovers 20/20 exact keys on a paired cohort without reconstructing the nibble partition. On those instances, our first-round route uses fewer live trace queries and less public table data. The exact quotient provides a concrete test for selector partitions that survive address enlargement.

item.title: Tight Depth Lower Bounds for Stretch Amplification
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2728
Authors: Oliver Korten
Summary: We investigate the depth overhead of stretch-amplification for pseudorandom generators in the black-box model. We show that any black box construction of a PRG $H: \{0,1\}^m \to \{0,1\}^M$ which makes $\mathrm{poly}(n)$ queries to a PRG $G: \{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}^N$ in $d$ adaptive phases during each evaluation (and with a black-box reduction to the security of $G$) must satisfy: $M \leq (m + O(\log n)) \Bigl( \frac{N}{n - O(\log n)} \Bigr)^d$. This implies that the standard amplification procedure [GM'84, GGM'86] based on repeated composition of $G$ is essentially optimal. In particular, amplifying $n \mapsto n+1$ to $m \mapsto 2m$ requires depth overhead $d = \Omega(\frac{n}{\log n})$, and amplifying $n \mapsto 2n$ to $m \mapsto m^2$ requires depth overhead $d = \Omega(\log n)$; each of these bounds is tight up to a constant factor. As an immediate corollary we obtain tight lower bounds on the depth complexity of black-box constructions of PRFs from PRGs. Both of these problems (pertaining to amplification and PRF construction) have been studied in various prior works [V'05, MV'11, BJP'11, MV'15, BMM'24, ADV'26]. Despite progress on special cases in which the structure of the reductions is constrained, it was previously unknown whether completely parallel constructions ($d=1$) existed in every stretch regime.
The kinds of amplification procedures we investigate have more recently found use outside of cryptography in the study of range avoidance ("Avoid") [K'21]. We show an analogous result in this setting: any black-box $\mathrm{FP^{NP}}$ reduction from an Avoid instance $G: \{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}^N$ to a second Avoid instance $H: \{0,1\}^m \to \{0,1\}^M$ which has "depth $d$" in the above sense must satisfy the same bound relating $n,N,m,M,d$. Using this impossibility result for Avoid, we construct an oracle relative to which $\mathrm{E} \not\subseteq \mathrm{NC}/\mathrm{poly}$ but $\mathrm{E^{NP}} \subseteq \mathrm{P}/\mathrm{poly}$. Our oracle separation implies that in the relativized setting, the bounded arithmetic theory $S^1_2$ cannot prove the existence of functions outside $\mathrm{P}/\mathrm{poly}$, even given as an axiom the existence of functions outside $\mathrm{NC}/\mathrm{poly}$.

item.title: On the (Quantum) Communication Complexity of Secure MPC from a Random Oracle
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2727
Authors: Alexander Hoover, Giuseppe Persiano, Kevin Yeo
Summary: Information-theoretic MPC among $n$ parties with $t$ corruptions can securely evaluate a circuit $C$ with $O(|C| \cdot t/(n-t))$ online communication in the preprocessing model and $O(|C| \cdot t/(n-2t))$ communication in the honest majority setting. Damg{\aa}rd, Larsen and Nielsen (CRYPTO 2019) showed that both communication bounds are tight for inner products. Fully homomorphic encryption and other assumptions known to imply public-key cryptography beat both communication bounds, but the communication complexity with symmetric-key cryptography alone is less understood. For MPC with preprocessing, we prove that the same $\Omega(|C| \cdot t/(n-t))$ lower bound holds in the random oracle model, so a random oracle cannot reduce the online communication. For honest majority MPC relative to a random oracle, we present an $\Omega(|C|)$ communication lower bound that is matched by a new construction for degree-2 polynomials (including inner products) when $n = O(\log \lambda)$, beating the information-theoretic bound.
We also study quantum MPC. First, we prove that information-theoretic protocols with quantum communication (and preprocessing) cannot reduce communication compared to their classical counterparts. Furthermore, we extend our lower bound for MPC with preprocessing to protocols with a quantum-accessible random oracle, but use only classical communication. In contrast, with both quantum communication and a post-quantum one-way function, we present a simple two-party protocol that evaluates the two-party instance of these circuits with $\mathsf{poly}(\lambda, \log |C|)$ communication, beating these lower bounds. Finally, such communication savings do not come for free. We prove that there exist circuits $C$ such that every blackbox protocol with $o(|C|)$ quantum communication must perform $\Omega(|C|)$ cryptographic operations.

item.title: Efficient Polynomial Multiplier Architectures for ML-KEM on Resource-Constrained FPGAs
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2726
Authors: Hossein Naderi Varandi, Raziye Salarifard
Summary: The Number Theoretic Transform (NTT) is a key component of polynomial multiplication in Kyber, making its efficient hardware implementation essential for post-quantum cryptographic applications. This paper presents two hardware architectures for Kyber polynomial arithmetic, supporting the NTT, inverse NTT (INTT) and point-wise multiplication (PWM) operations. The first architecture employs a single processing element (PE) to reduce hardware area, while the second uses two PEs to achieve higher throughput and efficiency. Both architectures incorporate a low-complexity modular multiplication and reduction method tailored to the Kyber modulus q = 3329, a unified butterfly unit supporting NTT, INTT, and PWM, and constant-geometry data access with dedicated address-generation algorithms. The dual-PE architecture is implemented without dedicated DSP blocks or BRAMs. FPGA implementation results demonstrate that the dual-PE architecture achieves the lowest area-time product and highest frequency among the evaluated state-of-the-art designs, while providing an effective trade-off between hardware area and execution time.

item.title: Complete Addition Law for Twisted Edwards Curves
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2725
Authors: Reza Rezaeian Farashahi, Ruhallah Mirzaei Aliarabi, Peyman Shahbazi Dastjerdi
Summary: We construct complete addition laws in extended coordinates for twisted Edwards curves \(E_{a,d}:ax^2+y^2=1+dx^2y^2\), where \(a,d\in K^\times\), \(a\ne d\), and \(\operatorname{char}K\ne2\). If \(t\in K\) makes \((t^2-a)(t^2-d)\) a nonzero nonsquare, the construction yields a \(K\)-complete formula valid for every pair of \(K\)-rational points. The proof describes the exceptional fibres through the difference morphism. Over finite fields of odd cardinality \(q>16\), such a coefficient exists for every nonsingular parameter pair, including the same-square-class cases with full rational two-torsion.
We give full and mixed evaluation schedules. Full addition costs \(8M+D_c\) in split elementary models and \(10M\) or \(12M\), plus fixed-constant costs, in the same-square-class cases. Doubling costs \(4M+4S+\min(D_a,D_d)\), independently of coefficient selection. Here \(M\) denotes a general field multiplication, \(S\) a squaring, and \(D_c\) multiplication by a fixed \(c\in K\).

item.title: Complete Addition on Short Weierstrass Curves with Point-Free Lines
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2724
Authors: Ruhallah Mirzaei Aliarabi, Reza Rezaeian Farashahi
Summary: Let $E_{a,b}:Y^2Z=X^3+aXZ^2+bZ^3$ be a nonsingular short-Weierstrass curve over a field $K$ of characteristic different from $2$ and $3$. A nonvertical line $Y=mX+nZ$ has no $K$-rational point on the curve if and only if $x^3-m^2x^2+(a-2mn)x+b-n^2$ is rootless in $K$. We give coordinate changes and formulas for the corresponding $K$-complete Bosma--Lenstra addition law. An incidence count proves that such a line exists over every finite field in the stated characteristic. The classical five-multiplication cross-product identity reduces the output computation by one multiplication. For normalized horizontal, sloped, and depressed families, the full/full costs are $13M+5D+30A$, $13M+5D+33A$, and $13M+(2\text{ to }5)D+60A$, respectively. Horizontal normalization requires a nonzero cube parameter; the depressed family always contains a point-free line over $\mathbb{F}_p$ for $p\ge47$. The zero-line formula costs $11M+3D_a+2D_{3b}+28A$ and is complete over finite $K$ exactly when $\#E(K)$ is odd. We also give complete doubling formulas, account for changes of coordinates, and apply the five-product identity to published Hessian addition formulas.

item.title: Distill and Conquer: Cryptanalytic Extraction of Local Rules in the Hard-Label Setting
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2723
Authors: Chun Li, Di Li, Liping Zhuang, Siqi Zhu, Yufeng Tang, Xingfu Yan, Zheng Gong
Summary: Cryptanalytic extraction can expose proprietary neural network parameters, but unknown architectures and large parameter counts complicate recovery under hard-label access. Local class-pair rules offer a narrower target by making class-switching conditions explicit and predicting nearby labels under a specified sampling law. Distillation methods mainly return substitute models rather than explicit rules whose local agreement has been tested against the victim. We propose Distill–Probe–Extract to produce such rules without first identifying the victim architecture. Verified boundary events guide student training, and student gradients propose directions at boundary anchors refined through victim queries. Fresh hard-label queries then test the proposed rules, retaining validation inputs and victim labels for each accepted rule. On a digits multilayer perceptron and pooling convolutional networks, fixed-candidate comparisons isolate the savings from replacing victim-normal estimation with student gradients. For the multilayer perceptron, median recorded online cost decreases from 246 to 118 queries per attempt after student preparation. With preparation and failures counted, full Fashion-MNIST sessions produce 2.03–2.23 times Direct's accepted-rule count under the original validation gate at 320,000-call caps. At 320,000 calls, a separate student-level test on trained Blended watermarks yields 99.99% trigger agreement and 91.79% clean agreement, with all three seeds passing joint verification.

item.title: Normal-Jet Masking: A Retraining-Free Defense Against Cryptanalytic Extraction of Neural Networks
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2722
Authors: Chun Li, Liping Zhuang, Di Li, Yufeng Tang, Ming Duan, Zheng Gong
Summary: Cryptanalytic extraction (CEA) of piecewise-linear neural networks recovers hidden signatures and parameters by locating critical points or hard-label dual points that expose off-manifold geometry. Proposed mitigation methods include query monitoring, output perturbation, ownership verification, and extraction-aware training. Train to Defend (TTD) directly addresses CEA through extraction-aware training, but cannot protect an already-trained checkpoint without retraining. We propose Normal-Jet Masking (NJM), a post-training wrapper that leaves the source model unchanged. NJM calibrates a tangent–normal tube around protected data, keeps private normal-direction mask channels inactive inside the tube, and mixes their piecewise-linear activations into served outputs outside it. NJM targets the shared evidence-acquisition stage rather than one attack implementation: mask events enter both raw-logit (soft-label) critical finding and hard-label dual finding before downstream signature and parameter recovery. Across seven MLPs, NJM reduces raw-logit evidence F1 by 53.8–93.1%, raises query cost by 1.4–9.3×, and eliminates pure hard-label duals. On CNNs, it preserves at least 0.9993 agreement while lowering source precision. These results show that post-training geometric masking complements training-time hardening across soft- and hard-label CEA.

item.title: Authenticated Outsourced Incrementally Verifiable MPC
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2721
Authors: Hamidreza Khoshakhlagh, Anders Kallesøe, Anders Dalskov
Summary: Many privacy-preserving applications such as iterative machine learning training require executing ongoing computations over a secret state for long periods of time. While MPC enables secure computation, long-lived secret state is vulnerable to adaptive corruptions, requiring periodic share refreshes and committee rotation. In many settings, it is desirable for external parties to be able to verify that these state updates and rotations are performed correctly, but existing approaches for such public verifiability incur high overhead as they require MPC nodes to generate expensive proofs over secret-shared data.
We propose Authenticated Outsourced Incrementally Verifiable MPC (IV-MPC), a framework for efficient public verification of long-running MPC computation. Our approach decouples private proof computation (run by MPC nodes) from public tasks within the proof generation that can be delegated to a single external prover $P^*$. To realize this architecture, we introduce three main components: (1) a Private-opening Polynomial Commitment Scheme (PoPCS) that lets an incoming committee prove they received the correct state shares without revealing the underlying data; (2) an efficient distributed proof system based on the sumcheck protocol and compressed $\Sigma$-protocols to verify state updates; and (3) a stateless handover technique that anchors committee transfers to a fixed state commitment, preventing proof sizes from growing over time. Combined with an incrementally verifiable computation (IVC) proof run by the external prover $P^*$, IV-MPC enables external auditors to verify correctness of MPC computation at every round with verification time asymptotically independent of the total number of epochs.

item.title: Unique Signature Schemes with Tight Security in the Random Oracle Model via Hash-and-Subset-Sign
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2720
Authors: Thomas Attema, Lisa Kohl, Joost van der Laan
Summary: Unique signatures are digital signature schemes, where each message has exactly one valid signature. The uniqueness property typically comes at a price: Most unique signature schemes are known to have a security loss at least linear in the number of signature queries when aiming for existential unforgeability under chosen message attacks (EUF-CMA) security, which was shown to be inherent in the standard model by Coron (EUROCRYPT 2002) for signature schemes where public keys are verifiable (i.e., where it can be efficiently checked whether a public key has unique signatures). The only known tight unique signature schemes in the literature that support verifiable public keys are variants of chain-based signatures (CRYPTO 2017, FC 2018, EUROCRYPT 2022), which achieve tight security in the random oracle model. To achieve constant security loss, however, these schemes require $\log q$ calls of the random oracle to sign and verify, where $q$ is an upper bound on the number of signatures generated using the scheme.
In this work, we provide the first tight unique signature scheme with verifiable public keys which requires only a constant number (namely, six) random oracle queries to sign and verify. Specifically, we provide a general transformation akin to hash-and-sign which transforms a signature scheme with much weaker security (a variant of random unforgeability) into an EUF-CMA secure scheme. Signatures of our resulting scheme consist of at most 3 sub-signatures in parallel.
Furthermore, we consider tightness in the multi-user setting, where the adversary may query signatures relative to many public keys, before deciding for which to forge. In this setting, we provide two constructions which achieve (1) a tight signature scheme, secure against semi-adaptive corruptions (i.e., where the adversary has to decide whether to corrupt a public key *before* making any signature queries relative to this key), and (2) a tight few-time signature scheme, secure against adaptive corruptions, where the scheme's setup is allowed to depend on an a-priori polynomial bound on the number of queries that the adversary has access to. These are the first unique signature schemes which are tightly secure in the multi-user model.

item.title: Construction and Classification of Minimum-Latency 5-Bit APN S-Boxes
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2719
Authors: Yaqi Qu, Xiutao Feng, Ruanyiyang Sun
Summary: S-boxes serve as essential nonlinear building blocks in symmetric-key cryptography, where their cryptographic properties and hardware implementation costs jointly dictate the security and efficiency of lightweight primitives. This paper studies the construction and classification of minimum-latency 5-bit APN (Almost Perfect Nonlinear) permutations under a prescribed gate-delay model, using exact minimum latencies of Boolean component functions.
Under the fixed gate-delay model of the NanGate 45nm standard cell library, we partition the search space into input-variable permutation (IP) equivalence classes to establish a comprehensive minimum-latency database covering all 5-input balanced nonlinear Boolean functions. This database delivers exact minimum latencies and gate-level implementations for all equivalence classes up to a latency of 150ps, while guaranteeing strict lower bounds on latency for classes exceeding that threshold, combining property filtering with circuit synthesis.
We search the five affine equivalence classes of 5-bit APN permutations. For each affine transformation of the input, we use exact component-function latencies to select components with linearly independent masks and choose their polarities, obtaining S-box circuits without repeating gate-level synthesis for each candidate. Exhaustive search with latency-preserving input-variable permutation reduction establishes a minimum latency of 126.745ps over all 5-bit APN permutations under the prescribed gate-delay model, with explicit constructions attaining this minimum in every class.The classification results give the optimized latency distributions and numbers of optimal IP classes of input-affine transformations within each affine class. Comparisons with selected 5-bit S-box implementations under the same model show simultaneous reductions in some cases: latency decreases by $10.20\%$--$29.18\%$ and normalized gate area by $5.37\%$--$27.69\%$, while preserving the original S-box mappings.

item.title: Revisiting Accountability in Accountable Tracing Signatures
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2718
Authors: Rei Naito, Kyoichi Asano, Keita Emura
Summary: Accountable tracing signatures (ATS), introduced by Kohlweiss and Miers (PoPETs 2015), classify each group member (user) as either traceable or non-traceable. A traceable user corresponds to one in conventional group signature schemes whose identity can be revealed by the opener from a signature, whereas a non-traceable user cannot be identified from any signature they produce. The opener, who issues a witness, can certify a user's status via the Account algorithm. In this paper, we formalize accountability soundness, which ensures that no two witnesses can simultaneously certify a user as both traceable and non-traceable. We show that the Kohlweiss-Miers ATS scheme admits conflicting witnesses that violate this property. Since accountability is a fundamental aspect of ATS, as reflected in its name, such conflicting witnesses undermine the intended guarantees of the primitive. To address this issue, we propose a patched version of the Kohlweiss-Miers ATS scheme that provides accountability soundness. We also discuss the applicability of our attack to the lattice-based ATS scheme (Ling et al., CT-RSA 2019) and the isogeny-based ATS scheme (Shaw-Dutta, Indocrypt 2021), together with preliminary investigations of possible countermeasures. We emphasize that all our attacks fall outside the original security models.

item.title: Verifiable Data on Bitcoin: FlatMerkle Commitments, Refutable Proofs, and FlatChecks
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2717
Authors: Sergio Demian Lerner
Summary: We give a method to publish data on Bitcoin and to verify properties of that data on Bitcoin itself, against a publisher who may lie. The data is a FlatMerkle file – a structured byte string whose ordinary SHA-256 supports logarithmic inclusion proofs and logarithmic proofs of malformation – placed in a transaction's annex or, at four times the cost but relayable by Bitcoin Core, in an output. We show that the publisher's ordinary Taproot signature, with a suitably chosen signature-hash type, binds the publisher to the published data in a form that a dispute can authenticate with a single SHA-256 compression plus the signature check, or with three compressions when no annex is used. Claims about the data, and claims about such claims, are published as proof messages in two formats: a plain encoding, refuted by revealing it whole, and a traced encoding that stores the verifier's output after each level, so that any false message is refuted by revealing at most five of its elements. The format, chosen by a cost model that weighs challenge bytes against published bytes, is fixed by public context so that no message can be read in two formats; chains of claims about claims settle at four logical elements. A dispute thus reduces to a few dozen SHA-256 compressions and one Schnorr verification per commitment – too large for Bitcoin Script, but small enough to adjudicate with an interactive bisection game, a chunked script in the manner of BitVM2, or a garbled circuit. The same technique verifies any locally refutable verifier, one whose every rejection is witnessed by a single check over a few words of a canonical trace. In a FlatCheck, the prover publishes only the proof; the trace, the verifier's intermediate values, is published only if a challenger asks for it, and the dispute then examines the single check he names. When the verifier splits into groups that each read a few parts of the proof, a challenge forces the trace of one group only. We give two examples: a toy L2 of signed transfers, whose 512-transfer batches cost 12,200 vbytes to claim, and a Bitcoin header-chain light client verified on Bitcoin itself, which claims a retarget period of 2,016 headers in 45,200 vbytes; a dispute over a local check costs about 37,500 and 49,200 vbytes, and one over a malformed trace about 77,100 and 99,800, independently of the number of groups. Verifying STARK proofs is another application. We also remove FlatMerkle's restriction to power-of-two sizes without padding.

item.title: Key Recovery Against RLCE via the GIJS Distinguisher
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2716
Authors: Jacob Alperin-Sheriff
Summary: We present an experimental cryptanalysis of the RLCE cryptosystem at the heretofore secure $w=n-k$ parameter regime. Our attack relies crucially on the recent Ghoshal--Ishai--Jain--Sun (GIJS) distinguisher The attack shortens the public key at random positions, runs the GIJS distinguisher with \emph{every} column as hold-out, and uses this distinguisher to identify twin pairs based on how they appear across trials. Three pairs so identified are unmixed by a root-finding cascade, and Sidelnikov--Shestakov on the resulting $k \times (k+3)$ pure matrix recovers the key.
We experimentally verify our attack by breaking the ID-0 (128-bit) in 30.5 core-hours (about 3 hours of wall time) on a standard higher-end laptop.

item.title: A Constant-Rate Compiler for Continual Memory Leakage
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2715
Authors: Shweta Agrawal, Anuja Modi, Rajeev Raghunath
Summary: Leakage-resilient compilers transform any computation so that physical leakage from its implementation reveals nothing beyond its input-output behaviour. In this work, we investigate this question in the well-motivated continual memory leakage (CML) model, that captures a variety of relevant real-world side-channel attacks and subsumes several other well studied models in the leakage domain. In this model with two independently leaking components (at least two are necessary), all known general compilers tolerate only an inverse-polynomial leakage-rate.
We give a compiler with constant leakage-rate, in the hybrid model with a simple inputless leak-free sampler as in Dziembowski and Faust (TCC 2012). It protects any deterministic computation on a fixed secret with public inputs and outputs, and comes with a transfer theorem: any security game in which the adversary has an oracle for the computation remains secure when every oracle call is replaced by a compiled evaluation that leaks continuously. Our compiler uses no computational assumption.
Our main application is public-key encryption. Applied to the decryption of any IND-CCA2 secure PKE, the compiler gives IND-CCLA2 security, i.e. CCA2 security even when every decryption leaks, including after the challenge ciphertext, with the same public key, ciphertexts and encryption algorithm. Instantiating the base scheme gives such PKE from LWE and from LPN improving upon the previous best post-quantum constructions in this model, which supported only inverse-polynomial leakage-rate. We also obtain signatures, PRFs and MACs with constant leakage-rate via a natural generalization.
Our key idea is to pack the entire configuration of a universal machine into one element of a large extension field, so that any computation keeps only a constant number of inner-product encodings in memory at any time, each for only a constant number of rounds. Our techniques are inspired by packing techniques in homomorphic encryption adapted to a completely different context. We are optimistic that our techniques will find other applications.

item.title: Polynomial Batch Accumulators for Onboarding-Dominant Zero-Knowledge Membership Proofs
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2714
Authors: Samanta Karmaker, Sampad Sikder, Md Ariful Islam, Md Sadek Ferdous
Summary: Zero-knowledge membership accumulators are conventionally tailored for slowly growing sets with frequent proof generation, creating severe efficiency bottlenecks for modern compliance architectures. Governance-driven applications like FATF customer due diligence, eIDAS 2.0 wallet issuance, and MiCA VASP authorization invert this structure. In this regime, rosters are ingested at an enterprise scale, while proofs are requested selectively. To resolve this mismatch, we introduce Polynomial Equation Batching (PEB), a membership accumulator for onboarding heavy workloads. PEB represents up to 128 members per batch as a characteristic polynomial and hashes its coefficients via Poseidon, seamlessly scaling to arbitrarily large populations through parallel batching. We present two variants: PEB-A, which maps member secrets directly to polynomial roots for maximum performance, and PEB-B, which hashes secrets in-circuit for hardened security. Implemented in Noir and Barretenberg on BN254, and evaluated for up to 1,048,576 members, PEB provides significant performance improvements. Compared to incremental Merkle trees, PEB-A achieves up to a 149.07x mean speedup in per-user initialization while incurring a modest 33.87% proof-generation overhead. Additionally, against static Merkle trees, PEB-A delivers a 15.71x speedup during setup. By shifting off-circuit overhead from hash evaluations to field multiplications, PEB provides a highly efficient, scalable solution for real-world zero-knowledge compliance systems.

item.title: CHAMPing at the Bit: Short Square-Root Collisions for Two-Generator Cayley Hashes
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2713
Authors: Freeman Slaughter
Summary: For $A,B\in\text{GL}(\mathbb{F}_p)$, a Cayley hash $\text{HM}(w)$ maps a bit string $w \in \{0,1\}$ to the corresponding product of $A$ and $B$. We construct collisions by finding two palindromes whose matrix products commute. A symmetric form shared by the two generators places the hash of every palindrome in a three-dimensional subspace containing the identity. Two such hashes commute when their traceless parts are proportional, which defines a class map with $p+2$ values, so the pigeonhole principle gives collisions of $4\lceil\log_2(p+3)\rceil$ bits. Under a uniformity heuristic, a dictionary search finds such a pair after about $\sqrt{\pi p/2}$ class evaluations. Adding one bit to each half-message gives an expected bound of $O(\sqrt p)$ evaluations, with no assumption on how the classes are distributed. When the common form is singular, the generators are simultaneously triangular and the same argument applies to ordinary words.
For CHAMP-512 and CHAMP-1024, the heuristic search finds collisions of $512$ and $1024$ bits after about $2^{64}$ and $2^{128}$ class evaluations, and the one-bit-longer, distribution-independent variant finds collisions of $516$ and $1028$ bits at the same leading cost. This matches the asymptotic cost of an earlier commuting-product search for CHAMP, whose messages have $O(\log^2(p))$ bits, and improves on the bound of about $p$ given by an earlier palindrome restriction. For every pair over an odd prime field, this also shortens the collisions of the general algorithm of Mullan and Tsaban from $O(\log^2(p)/\log(\log(p)))$ to $4 \lceil \log_2(p+3) \rceil$ bits. Since the argument applies to every pair $A,B$, no pair of generators gives a $2\times2$ Cayley hash over $\mathbb{F}_p$ with collision resistance greater than $O(\sqrt p)$. We give an explicit proof-of-concept collision for the CHAMP matrices at a $36$-bit prime, and prove that every sufficiently short message can be recovered from its digest for the main CHAMP pair. To close, we demonstrate that since reversal and symbol exchange act as sign changes on quaternion coordinates, the alternative CHAMP pair possesses a much greater degree of symmetry, but do not yet see how to utilize this to find collisions below the square-root bound.

item.title: Concrete Minimum Distance Bounds of Accumulate Codes over any Fixed Finite Field
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2712
Authors: Alexander R. Block, Himanshu Dongre, Hendrik Waldner
Summary: We present a new concrete unified distance analysis of three accumulate-type error-correcting codes over any finite field, specifically the Repeat-Accumulate (RA), Repeat-Accumulate-Accumulate (RAA), and Expand-Accumulate (EA) codes. For message length $k$, codeword length $n$, finite field size $q>2$, and target relative minimum distance $\delta$, we give new upper bounds on the probability that each of the above codes do not have minimum distance at least $\delta$. Our bounds are concrete and explicit: they do not rely on $n$ or $q$ being sufficiently large. We present (multiple) closed-form upper bounds on the failure probability for each code, and complement these bounds with asymptotic analyses that (nearly) match prior-known asymptotic bounds. Our technical core is a new fine-grained union bound for accumulate codes, which may be of independent interest, that examines inputs to the accumulator from a purely distributional perspective, deriving properties that are necessary for an input vector to accumulate to a targeted output weight, and analyzing the probability the input distribution achieves these properties. This fine-grained union bound generalizes the input-output weight enumerator approach used by many prior works.
Our concrete analysis shows that (1) the RA code has concretely small distance (a maximum of $\delta\leq 2.4979\times10^{-8}$ for $k=2^{40}$ and $q=2^{32}$, except with probability $2^{-60}$), and (2) the RAA and EA codes achieve somewhat large concrete distance for smaller field sizes $q \leq 2^{32}$. Concretely, for rate $k/n = 1/4$, $k\in\{2^{40},2^{50}\}$, and $q=2^{8}$, the RAA code has distance $\delta=1/8$ except with $2^{-60}$ probability, whereas the rate $1/2$ and $1/4$ EA code for the same $k$ and $q=2^{4}$, respectively, has distance $\delta\leq 0.0689756$ and $\delta \leq0.232955$ except with probability $2^{-60}$. For fields of size $q\geq 2^{32}$, under our concrete bounds, all codes experience a sharp drop-off in attainable minimum distance, as our analysis targets (small) fixed $q$.

item.title: Fast Provable Algorithms for Approximate CVP and Exact SVP on Random \(q\)-ary Lattices
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2711
Authors: Jiseung Kim, Junhyuk Kwon, Changmin Lee, JeongHwan Lee
Summary: We give provable randomized algorithms for the $\gamma$-approximate Closest Vector Problem ($\gamma$-CVP) with $\gamma=5/3$ and the exact Shortest Vector Problem (SVP) in the Euclidean norm on random $q$-ary lattices. These lattices consist of the integer vectors mapped to zero modulo $q$ by a uniformly random matrix $\mathbf{H}\in(\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z})^{m\times n}$, for any integer $q\ge2$. For input density $\delta=m\log_2q/n$ with $0\le\delta\le1$, the running times are $2^{0.2668n+o(n)}$ for $5/3$-CVP and $2^{0.2741n+o(n)}$ for exact SVP, with polynomial input-length factors suppressed. For $1<\delta\le3/2$, the respective bounds are $2^{0.56n+o(n)}$ and $2^{0.468n+o(n)}$. For all but a negligible fraction of matrices, both algorithms succeed with overwhelming probability over their internal randomness. Notably, for $0\le\delta\le1$, our provable bounds fall below even the $2^{0.2925n+o(n)}$ heuristic estimate for classical lattice sieving.
As a cryptographic application, we prove that signatures in the original construction of Gentry, Peikert, and Vaikuntanathan (GPV) can be forged in time $2^{0.0534n+o(n)}$ for $n\ge5m\log_2q$. For a $128$-bit security target, a leading-term estimate gives $n\approx2400$ and a public key of roughly $144$ kB, indicating a substantial storage burden.

item.title: Hidden Curves and Short Duals: Cubic Jets, Dual Leaks, and the Limits of Masked-Code Encryption
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2710
Authors: Yongge Wang
Summary: Masked-code encryption hides a decodable code behind a transformation meant to make it look random. We study the two masks proposed as compact alternatives to Goppa codes---Wang's RLCE and the $(U\,|\,U{+}V)$ construction of UVW-KEM---over the decodable hidden codes they have been or could be applied to, and find that, among the families examined, none yields a compact trapdoor.
Over Reed--Solomon and algebraic-geometry codes the mask hides a \emph{curve}, and curves are not hidden from jets. We explain the October 2026 key recovery of UVW-KEM (NGCC) and show it is not specific to UVW: for \emph{hidden-pairing codes} we bound from below the dependencies among order-$r$ jets of degree-$d$ forms at the columns of any shortening---for cubics $2k_1-k_2-k_l+2$ (UVW) and $2(n{-}k)-w-k_l+2$ (RLCE), attained in every regime tested, and we prove that the structured part of the dependency space carries the pairing and the secret ratios in closed form. Every proposed UVW parameter set has the predicted cubic deficiency (key recovery has been demonstrated at UVW-KEM-128). RLCE's long-key regime $w\ge n-k$, out of reach of the square-code attack for eight years, falls at degree three: on a full-size Level-1 parameter set we recover an equivalent key from the public key alone and decrypt fresh ciphertexts. HermitianRLCE is distinguished the same way. A forcing law, a master count and a redundancy law make the \emph{jet degree} an invariant of hidden-pairing codes: within that model, each unit of structural depth costs a unit of redundancy.
Without a curve the masks fail differently: both \emph{preserve the dual} of the hidden code, at most doubling the weight of every dual word. polarRLCE at rate $\le2/3$ leaks dual words found in $47$--$94$ bits; at higher rates no certified decoding radius supports $143$-bit security up to length $16384$, and at $32768$ the key is $58$\,MiB, $234\times$ Classic McEliece. LDPC codes leak their sparse checks, MDPC codes are better left unmasked, and UVW carries a matched-pair subspace for every hidden code. Reed--Muller-heavy codes under RLCE resist every attack here at $4$\,MiB keys, but only if a decoder at $3.4\times$ the bounded-distance radius exists.

item.title: Private Accounts Without $O(N)$ Work Through a Hybrid State Model
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2709
Authors: Philipp Gackstatter, François Garillot, Marti Górny, Adrian Hamelink, Al Kindi, Philippe Laferrière, Robin Salen, Brian Seong, Bobbin Threadbare
Summary: Privacy-preserving smart contracts face a scalability problem. In account-balance-vector designs, hiding which accounts changed requires that every transaction perform an indistinguishable update over the global state, so validators pay work linear in the number of accounts for every private transfer. UTXO systems avoid this by validating local spends, but do not provide the same account-style programming model.
We argue that the usual "account vs.~UTXO" framing conflates state representation and execution model, two choices that can be made separately. Miden, an Ethereum Layer 2, separates them. It uses persistent accounts for programmability, asynchronous notes for value transfer, and client-side proving for execution. Validators verify proofs and update commitments without re-executing transactions or accessing uninvolved state.
The result is an account-based platform with private transfers and private computation, while keeping validator work per transaction logarithmic in the number of accounts.

item.title: Beyond Standard Indifferentiability: Simulator Properties for Fiat-Shamir Security
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2708
Authors: Ashrujit Ghoshal, Sikhar Patranabis
Summary: The Fiat-Shamir transform converts public-coin interactive arguments into non-interactive arguments (NARGs). Its security is typically analyzed in the random-oracle model, while implementations instantiate the random oracle with structured hash constructions. Standard indifferentiability is the natural abstraction for justifying this replacement. Chiesa and Orru (TCC ’25), however, showed that standard indifferentiability does not generally preserve the information and reset behavior needed by common Fiat-Shamir extraction arguments, and proposed stronger notions of indifferentiability to bridge this gap.
We show that standard indifferentiability can nevertheless be retained as the oracle-replacement abstraction. For knowledge soundness, we give generic transfer theorems for three extraction interfaces: proof-only straight-line extraction follows from standard indifferentiability alone; transcript-dependent extraction additionally requires transcript reconstruction; and rewinding extraction requires reconstruction for rewinding, preserving simulator behavior across invocations with the same hidden randomness. Our results apply to worst-case polynomial-time extractors. Moreover, we show that the rewinding requirement is inherent: assuming discrete-logarithm hardness, we construct a perfectly indifferentiable construction and fixed prover admitting error-free rewinding extraction in the ideal world, while every polynomial-time construction-world extractor succeeds only with negligible probability.
We instantiate our framework for tagged prefix-free Merkle-Damgard and a fixed-output permutation sponge. The former admits exact transcript and rewinding reconstruction, while the latter admits exact transcript reconstruction and rewinding reconstruction with negligible statistical error incurred only once, independently of the number of restarts.
For zero knowledge, we give a semantic formulation where one persistent simulator jointly generates the proof and public-oracle interaction. Here, standard indifferentiability alone yields a generic transfer theorem, requiring neither reconstruction property and incurring only the indifferentiability error. Thus standard indifferentiability provides a common oracle-replacement abstraction for knowledge soundness and semantic zero knowledge, with extraction-specific requirements isolated as separate simulator properties.

item.title: Poly Versus Polyval
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2707
Authors: Kaushik Nath, Palash Sarkar
Summary: We revisit the basic construction of polynomial evaluation based hash function, which we call Poly, over binary extension fields $GF(2^n)$, where $n=64k$ and $k\geq 2$. Unlike GHASH, the NIST standard polynomial evaluation based hash function for $n=128$, Poly does not perform the unnecessary bit reversals of each $n$-bit block, and consequently is faster than GHASH. Further, Poly differs from Polyval, -- a faster alternative to GHASH, -- in that Poly performs usual reduction, while Polyval performs Montgomery reduction. We identify suitable choices of the field representing irreducible polynomials which make usual and Montgomery reductions efficient. We provide detailed algorithms, and associated proofs of correctness for both kinds of reductions. Based on the algorithms, we report carefully optimised assembly implementation of both Poly and Polyval for $n=128,256$ and $512$. Our theoretical analysis and experimental timing results show that for $n=128$, Polyval is faster than Poly, while for $n=256$ and $512$ (as well as for higher values of $n$), Poly is faster than Polyval. The cases $n=128$ and $n=256$ are of current relevance due to the ongoing NIST process for developing cryptographic accordions.

item.title: Anamorphic Proofs of Knowledge from Prover Randomness
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2706
Authors: Zhi Lu, Songfeng Lu, Jiaheng Zhang
Summary: Anamorphic encryption and signatures deliver a hidden message through a normal-looking ciphertext or signature. We move from hidden messages to hidden knowledge claims and introduce anamorphic proofs of knowledge, in which a single proof certifies its normal statement publicly while convincing a designated checker that the prover knows a witness for a separately registered anamorphic statement, such as a long-term credential. Our construction reuses a commitment the normal prover already makes to its own randomness. The prover adds a secret mask to the anamorphic witness and uses the sum as those coins, so the existing commitment carries the anamorphic statement while the public statement, proof format and length, and normal verifier remain unchanged. Two properties of the normal proof system suffice: its randomness commitment must be extractable, and the complete proof must be simulatable at a commitment that the checking key fixes in advance, which normal zero knowledge does not provide. The resulting normal and anamorphic modes are indistinguishable to an external observer, even given both witnesses and the normal prover's actual random coins. The same opening extractor gives anamorphic knowledge soundness and two guarantees against the checker: it cannot produce an accepting proof for a statement registered independently of its key, and it cannot produce a proof and witness for a statement of its own choice, in both cases at an unused label and after obtaining honest proofs at other labels. The checker learns neither witness. We instantiate the construction in random-base Compressed $\Sigma$ and in Bulletproofs with range aggregation in the random-oracle model. Finally, we show that three-move protocols with witness-assisted challenge transfer, including Schnorr and uncompressed representation protocols, cannot support the primitive in a local-checking model.

item.title: SpreadMAYO: Unlocking Greater Parallelism for Faster MAYO Signatures on GPUs
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2705
Authors: Zhuoyu Xie, Tian Zhou, Fangyu Zheng, Yijing Ning, Yi Bian, Wangchen Dai, Jiankuo Dong, Yuewu Wang, Jingqiang Lin, Jiwu Jing
Summary: Quantum computing threatens public-key cryptography, motivating post-quantum signature standardization. MAYO, a multivariate Round 3 candidate in NIST's additional signature process, offers compact keys and signatures. However, prior GPU implementations do not fully exploit parallelism within each MAYO operation: equation-slice partitioning serializes independent matrix work, while signing requires frequent synchronization among threads during linear-system construction and elimination. We present SpreadMAYO, a high-throughput GPU implementation of MAYO Round 3 that exposes greater parallelism and reduces synchronization through finer task partitioning and a revised signing pipeline. SpreadMAYO distributes matrix contractions across rows, output positions, and 64-bit limbs while reusing operands in registers. Each limb packs sixteen GF(16) coefficients; native 32-bit operations process its halves without lookup tables. For signing, threads privately accumulate columns with deferred polynomial reduction, transpose packed columns into rows using warp shuffles, and eliminate rows below each pivot in parallel. Additionally, we employ a hybrid AES design to accommodate different workloads and fuse key expansion with matrix computations to reduce global-memory traffic. On an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090, SpreadMAYO outperforms the Round 3 adapted GPU baseline by 2.33–3.71× in key generation, 4.40–6.93× in signing, and 3.42–5.13× in verification, reaching up to 10.75× in repeated-key server signing.

item.title: Card-Based Protocols with Mixed Encoding: Computable Functions and the Minimum Number of Cards
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2704
Authors: Saeki Koizumi, Xiao-Nan Lu, Hidetomo Nabeshima
Summary: Card-based cryptography performs secure computation with physical cards, where a bit is usually encoded by two cards but can also be encoded by a single card. We study mixed encoding, in which one player gives a single-card commitment and the other a two-card commitment, for perfectly secure protocols with finite runtime and public actions. Mizuki (Theoretical Computer Science, vol.~622, 2016) proposed an AND protocol with mixed encoding as a building block for the conjunction of many variables. To give a single-card commitment, a player chooses one of two cards of different types and must keep the other card hidden. We call this card a frozen card and include it in the number of cards. We show that a secure protocol in committed format never turns over a single-card input, and use this to determine the functions that can be computed when all inputs are single-card commitments and to characterize those that can be computed with mixed encoding, which include AND but not XOR. We prove that Mizuki's five-card protocol is card-minimal. No AND protocol with mixed encoding uses four cards, including the frozen card, even with arbitrary shuffles and a non-committed output. For formal verification, we express the existence of a protocol as a quantified Boolean formula (QBF) in which security is a quantifier alternation, and confirm this lower bound with QBF solvers for a class of protocols. We discuss the number and type of shuffles, and analyze Mizuki's protocol under injection attacks that change only the input.

item.title: Efficient Scalable Oversight via Rewinding
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2703
Authors: Ziyi Guan, Yael Tauman Kalai, Ron Rothblum, Zoe Xi
Summary: Scalable oversight asks how a weak verifier can check the outputs of computations performed by more powerful AI systems. One proposed approach uses relativizing interactive proofs, in which a weak verifier checks the output of a complex oracle-aided computation by interacting with one or more powerful provers. A prominent example is debate, which is highly efficient but assumes that one of two powerful AI models, or provers, is truthful. For certain classes of oracle-aided computations, this assumption can be removed, but at substantially greater computational cost.
In this work, we introduce \emph{rewindable interactive proofs} (RIPs), a new model of relativizing interactive proofs for scalable oversight. In an RIP, the verifier may rewind the prover to an earlier state of the interaction and continue from there. This is possible when the prover is an AI model, since the verifier can save a snapshot of the model's state and later restore it. We construct a relativizing RIP for computations whose outputs are robust to changing a small fraction of oracle answers. Our construction is more efficient than prior relativizing proofs that do not assume a truthful prover, and it uses no cryptography.
In our construction the honest prover runs in time linear in that of the original computation, and the verifier, after a one-time preprocessing step, runs in time nearly linear in the input length (which can be much smaller than the computation itself). We implement our protocol, report a preliminary MNIST experiment, and show that an RIP can be faster than a state-of-the-art deployed proof system.
RIPs may be of independent interest. Rewinding is possible whenever the verifier controls the prover's machine, for example when the prover runs on trusted hardware or in a virtual machine whose state can be checkpointed.

item.title: The Authentication Complexity of Byzantine Consensus
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2702
Authors: Kecheng Shi
Summary: Byzantine broadcast and Byzantine agreement are fundamental problems in distributed computing and building blocks for secure multiparty computation. In complete synchronous networks of $n$ parties with channels identifying the immediate sender, classical results establish how authentication changes resilience to $t$ Byzantine faults. Without initially authenticated public keys, both tasks are possible if and only if $n>3t$~\cite{PSL80}. With a complete public-key infrastructure (PKI), broadcast tolerates every $t2t$. These thresholds leave a substantial gap: \emph{how much initial authentication is necessary for a given fault bound, and how does its distribution affect feasibility?}
We study this question by allowing each party's designated public verification key to be initially authenticated to any subset of the other parties. We represent this setup by a directed authentication graph $G$ whose vertices are parties, with an edge $x\to y$ exactly when $y$ is a \emph{verifier} of $x$: that is, $x$'s designated public verification key is initially authenticated to $y$. We count each edge as one unit and define \emph{authentication complexity} as the \emph{minimum} total bindings over all setups and protocols achieving the required task and fault tolerance. Protocols may establish further authentication during execution without adding initial cost.
We give a tight graph characterization of the initial authentication setups that support agreement, including when each party knows only its own initial key table and is not given the authentication graph. For $2t<n\le3t$ and $r=n-2t$, we show that agreement has authentication complexity $\Theta(\min\{n^2,(n^2/r)\ln(en/r)\})$ and give a protocol with polynomial local computation. At $n=2t+1$, broadcast requires $\Omega(n\ln^2 n/\ln\ln n)$ initial authentications, and has a construction using $O(n^{3/2}\sqrt{\ln n})$ initial authentications. At this threshold, we also show a complete PKI setup is necessary for agreement. Surprisingly, broadcast has subquadratic authentication complexity even when $t=n/2+o(n)$. For every fixed fault fraction $\alpha\in(1/2,1)$, we show its authentication complexity is $\Theta_\alpha(n^2)$. We also determine the exact authentication complexity of broadcast at maximum resilience: $\binom n2-1$ initial authentications suffice and are necessary to tolerate $t=n-1$ faults.

item.title: SPIDER: A Faster and Smaller Identity-Based Signature From Isogenies
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2701
Authors: Tako Boris Fouotsa, Gustave Tchoffo Saah
Summary: PRISM is an isogeny-based digital signature whose security relies on the problem of computing large prime degree isogenies from a supersingular elliptic curve of unknown endomorphism ring. In this paper, we design SPIDER, a digital signature that builds on a sigma protocol which when given a supersingular elliptic curve $E$, proves the knowledge of an isogeny $\phi: E\rightarrow E'$ of prime (or non smooth) degree $d$. SPIDER can hence be seen as a proof of knowledge of a PRISM signature. The latter observation allows us to combine SPIDER and PRISM to obtain an Identity-Based Signature (IBS) which we denote by SPIDER-IBS. SPIDER-IBS is the most efficient and the most compact isogeny-based IBS scheme, as all its predecessors are based on isogeny group actions.

item.title: Practical Collision Attacks on 22- and 23-Step SM3 (Preliminary Version)
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2700
Authors: Sitong Yuan, Haorui Cui, Hongbo Yu
Summary: SM3 is a 256-bit cryptographic hash function specified in the Chinese national standard GB/T 32905-2016 and the international standard ISO/IEC 10118-3:2018. In this paper, we present practical collisions for 22- and 23-step SM3 with the standard initial value. Compared with the 20-step collision result of Mendel et al. (2013), our constructions cover two and three additional steps, respectively. The time complexities are approximately \(2^{52.4}\) and \(2^{54.5}\) evaluations of 22- and 23-step SM3, respectively. We also present a semi-free-start collision for 24-step SM3.

item.title: Registered Functional Encryption with Certified Everlasting Security
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2699
Authors: Shayeef Murshid, Ramprasad Sarkar, Mriganka Mandal
Summary: Registered functional encryption removes the trusted authority bottleneck of standard functional encryption by allowing users to register their own public keys, with a transparent aggregation procedure producing a compact master public key. On the other hand, certified everlasting deletion enables a recipient to produce a classical certificate guaranteeing that a ciphertext has been information-theoretically destroyed, even against computationally unbounded adversaries. In this work, we initiate the study of registered functional encryption with certified everlasting deletion (RFE-CED), combining both properties for the first time. We define the syntax and security of RFE-CED, capturing two complementary guarantees: everlasting privacy, which bounds the trace distance between residual adversarial states after certified deletion, and post-verification indistinguishability, which ensures the adversary cannot distinguish the encrypted message even after the deletion certificate is verified. To construct RFE-CED, we also introduce public-slot registered functional encryption (PS-RFE) as a building block, in which each registered function takes both a secret and an arbitrary public input. Combining PS-RFE with a pseudorandom and authenticated BB84 encodings, we obtain a secure slotted RFE-CED scheme with the help of an interactive version of certified everlasting lemma.

item.title: Batched Threshold Predicate Encryption from Succinct LWE
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2697
Authors: Shayeef Murshid, Ramprasad Sarkar, Mriganka Mandal
Summary: Predicate encryption extends attribute-based encryption by providing fine-grained access control while hiding the attribute associated with a ciphertext beyond what the secret keys held by an adversary necessarily reveal. Batched identity-based encryption enables authorization with respect to a designated collection of identities. We introduce batched threshold predicate encryption (BT-PE), which combines batch-scoped authorization, expressive predicate-based access control, and threshold decryption. We give a lattice-based construction supporting polynomial-size arithmetic-circuit predicates, compact batch digests, and compact per-party key shares. Decryption is possible only when the encrypted attribute belongs to the authorized batch, satisfies the required predicate, and a sufficiently large set of parties participates. We prove correctness and query-selective one-sided security under the $\ell$-succinct LWE assumption, together with standard assumptions on digital signatures and compute-and-compare obfuscation.

item.title: Batched Identity-Based Encryption with Succinct Publicly Verifiable Subset Deletion
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2698
Authors: Shayeef Murshid, Ramprasad Sarkar, Mriganka Mandal
Summary: Batched identity-based encryption (BIBE) compresses a bounded set of identities into a succinct public digest, and provides a single secret key for decrypting ciphertexts associated with identities in the set. We introduce batched identity-based encryption with succinct publicly verifiable subset deletion (BIBE-SPVD), which allows a holder of polynomially many quantum ciphertexts to certify deletion of any chosen subset using a single succinct classical certificate while preserving the usability of the remaining ciphertexts. We first construct a classical BIBE from identity-based encryption with puncturable master secret key, somewhere statistically binding (SSB) hashing, and indistinguishability obfuscation. We then equip this scheme with publicly verifiable certified-everlasting deletion, using a generic compiler specialized to the BIBE functionality. Finally, individual deletion certificates are aggregated using a somewhere-extractable batch argument. For each ciphertext position, the corresponding statement requires a valid deletion certificate precisely when that position belongs to the deleted subset. The identity digest and batch key remain succinct, and for \(N\) ciphertexts the aggregate deletion certificate has size \(poly(\lambda,\log N)\), independent of the number deleted.

item.title: Ratio-Based Ring Oscillator PUF Statistical Model
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2696
Authors: Ondřej Staníček, Jiří Buček, Róbert Lórencz
Summary: A ratio-based ring oscillator physical unclonable function (ROPUF) provides high reliability and is capable of extracting multiple bits from a single ring oscillator pair. However, the derivation of the response bits from such PUFs and the assessment of their randomness have relied only on empirical statistical tests.
This paper introduces a novel, mathematically derived closed-form statistical model that characterizes the counter value distribution of the ratio-based ROPUF and formally describes the behavior of this PUF design. We empirically validate the model's assumptions using a large-scale real-world ring oscillator measurement dataset of 218 Xilinx Artix-7 FPGAs.
We demonstrate that this statistical framework enables theoretical quantification of response entropy of the ratio-based ROPUF. Furthermore, the model unlocks the use of advanced bit derivation methods, such as Equiprobable Quantization and Two-Metric Helper Data schemes. These were previously inapplicable to this PUF architecture, and we empirically show on the real-world dataset that they achieve better combinations of PUF reliability, randomness, and bit yield than the original counter-based derivation.

item.title: Short Collisions Separate Sponge from Merkle-Damgård
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2695
Authors: Ashrujit Ghoshal
Summary: We study short collisions in salted Merkle-Damg{\aa}rd (MD) and Sponge under the query-bounded preprocessing model introduced by Ghoshal and Tessaro (CRYPTO '23). The adversary makes at most $T_1$ oracle queries before a random salt is revealed and at most $T_2$ queries afterwards, and must output two colliding messages of at most $B$ blocks.
Our main result is a separation between the two constructions. Let $N=2^n$, give MD and Sponge matching $n$-bit salts, message blocks, and outputs, and set $T_1=\Theta(N/T_2)$ with $T_2=o(\sqrt N)$. For Sponge, there is an attack that finds a collision with constant probability using only three-block messages. In contrast, every MD adversary restricted to $B=o(T_2)$ blocks succeeds with probability at most \[ O\left(\frac{B}{T_2}+\frac{T_2^2}{N}\right)=o(1). \] Thus, under the same query budgets, three blocks suffice for Sponge, while every MD adversary with $B=o(T_2)$ blocks has success probability $o(1)$.
On the MD side, we prove an upper bound for arbitrary block bounds $B$. The proof uses a simple graph argument that distinguishes collisions already present in the preprocessing transcript from those that can actually be reached by a short computation starting from the subsequently sampled salt. This extends query-bounded preprocessing analysis beyond the previously understood one- and two-block cases.
On the Sponge side, we give a three-block attack that uses inverse permutation queries to make one precomputed collision useful from many different capacities. We complement the attack with a matching upper bound in a range containing the separation. In this range, allowing longer messages gives no asymptotic improvement: the optimal Sponge preprocessing advantage is already attained with at most three blocks.
Overall, our results show that collision length interacts fundamentally differently with preprocessing in the two constructions: under matched parameters and identical query budgets, Sponge admits constant probability three-block collisions, whereas MD does not achieve constant success for any $B=o(T_2)$.

item.title: Quantum Time-Space Tradeoffs for Short Merkle-Damgård Collisions
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2694
Authors: Shashwat Agrawal, Ashrujit Ghoshal, Venkata Koppula
Summary: We study time-space tradeoffs for finding short collisions in Merkle-Damg{\aa}rd~(MD) hashing in the quantum auxiliary-input quantum random-oracle model~(QAI-QROM). An adversary may preprocess the compression function into $S$ qubits of arbitrary oracle-dependent quantum advice and, after receiving a fresh salt, make $T$ superposition queries to find a collision consisting of at most $B$ blocks.
Previous quantum analyses gave an $\widetilde{O}(ST^3/N)$ security bound for MD collisions with classical advice. Unlike the classical theory of short MD collisions, however, this bound is insensitive to the collision length $B$: existing quantum techniques did not exploit the combinatorial structure forced by a short collision.
We develop a structure-sensitive compressed-oracle analysis that overcomes this obstacle. For two-block collisions, we prove an upper bound \[ \widetilde{O}\left(\min\left\{1, \frac{ST^2+T^3}{N}\right\}\right), \] even against arbitrary quantum advice. For $M=N$, together with the known attack, this gives a tight characterization up to logarithmic factors, closes the previous factor-$T$ gap in the preprocessing term, and resolves an open problem of Akshima, Guo, and Liu~(CRYPTO '22, JoC '24).
For general $B\le T$, we show in the regime $(2S+1)(T+2B)^3\le N$ that the success probability is at most \[ \widetilde{O}\!\left(\min\left\{1, \frac{ST^2B+T^3}{N}\right\}\right). \] Thus, when $B\ll T$, the preprocessing term improves over the previous $ST^3/N$ bound by a factor of roughly $T/B$. Motivated by the tight two-block result, we propose the $ST^2B$ conjecture, asserting that $ST^2B=\widetilde{\Theta}(N)$ is the correct constant-success tradeoff for short MD collisions in the regime $T^3=o(N)$.

item.title: Rotom: A Microcontroller-Oriented Tweakable Block Cipher Using Modular Multiplication (Full Version)
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2693
Authors: Kento Morita, Kazuhiko Minematsu, Kosei Sakamoto, Kazuma Taka, Rei Ueno, Takanori Isobe
Summary: We propose Rotom, a family of 128-bit tweakable block ciphers designed for efficient software implementation on 32-bit microcontrollers. The central design idea is to use modular multiplication as a compact and software-efficient source of strong nonlinearity. Rotom instantiates this idea with a fixed 16-bit S-box built from odd constant multiplication modulo $2^{16}$ interleaved with lightweight linear maps, and combines it with a software-friendly recursive linear layer over four 32-bit words, a compact tweakey schedule, and modular-addition boundary key mixing. In contrast to typical ARX-based ciphers, Rotom provides explicit differential and linear characteristic bounds by design. These bounds are obtained by exhaustively computing the local transition probabilities of its fixed 16-bit S-box and combining them with active-S-box bounds induced by its recursive linear layer. Implementation results on ARM Cortex-M3 and Cortex-M4 show that Rotom achieves cycle counts close to Speck, substantially lower than those of MSX, and faster than representative fixsliced AES implementations, while providing tweak support and cipher-level differential and linear bounds. Overall, Rotom combines the efficiency of software-oriented arithmetic instructions with the explicit security evaluation enabled by a fixed-S-box structure.

item.title: Efficient Implementations of Small-Modulus Lattice KEM Components
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2692
Authors: Ying Liu, Yu Zhang, Xianhui Lu
Summary: Small moduli support compact polynomial representations in lattice-based key encapsulation mechanisms (KEMs), including BAT (TCHES 2022) and END (ASIACRYPT 2026, to appear). However, compact encodings can be costly to convert, and uniform generation must account for both coefficient-extraction cost and random-bit demand. Incomplete number-theoretic transforms also leave residual polynomial products. To address these costs, we exploit the structure of moduli 257 and 769 to improve encoding, uniform public polynomial generation, and polynomial multiplication.
At $q=257$, we introduce zero-selector encoding: zero payload bytes locate ambiguous coefficients, and selector bits resolve their values. We analyze selector capacity, overflow, and key-generation retries. For $n=1024$, a 1033-byte configuration has overflow probability at most $2^{-128}$ under independent uniform coefficients. Checked AVX2 decoding takes 213 cycles, compared with 2203 cycles for BAT's 1040-byte format. At $q=769$, we lower conversion costs using an existing compact radix format at the same encoded length as BAT. We specialize rejection sampling to simplify coefficient extraction at $q=257$ and reduce random-bit demand at $q=769$. At $(q,n)=(769,1024)$, expected candidate-bit demand decreases by 24.39\% relative to direct 10-bit rejection. Four-polynomial generation uses 7.14-13.21\% fewer AVX2 cycles. For residual multiplication, proven range bounds justify omitting strict input-centering corrections, while register scheduling reduces stack accesses.
We integrate the public-key codecs and multiplication components into BAT and END. Across the tested C and AVX2 implementations, encapsulation costs decrease by $39.93-55.25\%$ in BAT and $41.36-48.84\%$ in END. The corresponding decapsulation reductions are $5.42-8.55\%$ in BAT and, for END, $23.99-45.89\%$ in C and $6.98-8.04\%$ in AVX2. END AVX2 gains mainly come from the public key codec. These results quantify the effect of modulus-specific optimizations on complete component and KEM costs.

item.title: Revisiting Hash-ECB-Hash Enciphering: Plaintext Recovery Attacks on PEP and TET
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2691
Authors: Hailun Yan, Yuexing Yue, Yaobin Shen, Peng Wang, Siwei Sun
Summary: Storage encryption motivates tweakable enciphering schemes, which encrypt entire multi-block data units without length expansion and use a public tweak to identify their context. We revisit PEP (FSE 2006) and TET (CRYPTO 2007), two Hash-ECB-Hash schemes that combine parallel block-cipher calls with invertible mixing, and present classical distinguishing and plaintext-recovery attacks. For PEP, we exhibit a fixed public field satisfying the published parameter-selection rule whose generated position coefficients repeat. This yields a two-query algebraic distinguisher and recovery of a secret tweak-derived value using one encryption query. For the same instance, we recover target plaintexts over a specified range of complete-block lengths using at most nine encryption queries and one decryption query. Our PEP success bounds assume a uniformly random secret permutation and independently fixed target tweaks and plaintexts. For TET, we analyze two corrections of a previously reported mismatch between encryption and decryption. Both admit two-query distinguishers on messages with a partial final block. For tails of at least two bits, we obtain deterministic plaintext recovery using two decryption queries in one correction, or two encryption queries and one decryption query in the other. These TET attacks hold for every data permutation and valid parameter choice. The results expose failures of concrete coefficient generation and partial-block processing, and identify requirements for repairing these constructions.

item.title: Weir: Bounded-Memory Indexing and Proving with Sequential Storage
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2689
Authors: Kyeongtae Lee, Jihye Kim, Hyunok Oh
Summary: A low-memory prover must control sumcheck tables, sparse accesses, commitments and proof assembly. We present Weir, a Shockwave-derived protocol with a complete read-write (RW) index-and-prove schedule. The schedule restores sparse request order, retains commitment state through later openings and assembles the proof externally. These steps preserve the direct RAM prover's canonical bytes across buffer choices, with a common verifier. Under an external-query-tape model, the schedule uses $O(B+\log T)$ field RAM, constant digest RAM and polylogarithmic auxiliary RAM. Algebraic work and record traffic are quasilinear; oracle-query byte work is charged separately. A classical random-oracle analysis bounds knowledge error.
Fused Split-Butterfly-Merge removes $n-1$ materialized transform passes at length $2^n$. Its ordered routing contract extends to multiplicative-coset Reed-Solomon (RS) and recursive foldable encoders; component checks match reference codewords, traffic counts and RS fold states. In a fixed 64 MiB worker-cap grid, RW completes all tested matrix and Poseidon inputs; RAM completes matrix dimension 8. Within the matrix grid, the largest RW point has 64 times as many padded constraints as that RAM point, using 3.33 MB prover RSS and 9.51 minutes index+prove. We report latency, external payload, query bytes, proof size and verification time for this offline operating range.

item.title: Gaussian Difference Dynamics: Breaking the $2^{n/2}$ Barrier for the Shortest Vector Problem and Discrete Gaussian Sampling
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2690
Authors: Yiming Gao, Xuyuan Han, Honggang Hu
Summary: We give classical randomized algorithms in a word-RAM model that break the $2^{n/2}$ barrier for both discrete Gaussian sampling (DGS) and the Shortest Vector Problem (SVP). For every fixed $\alpha>1$, shifted DGS on arbitrary lattices at width $\sigma\ge\alpha\eta_{1/2}(L)$ takes $$ (3/2)^{n/2+o(n)}\text{ time} \qquad\text{and}\qquad (4/3)^{n/2+o(n)}\text{ space}. $$ These bounds match the Becker--Ducas--Gama--Laarhoven (BDGL) heuristic sieving exponents. At widths at least $3\eta_{1/2}(L)/2$, the same total cost suffices for an entire batch of $\lfloor(4/3)^{n/2}\rfloor$ samples jointly close to independent target Gaussians.
For SVP on arbitrary lattices, our algorithm returns a shortest nonzero vector with high probability in $$ 2^{0.4130n+o(n)}\text{ time} \qquad\text{and}\qquad 2^{0.3138n+o(n)}\text{ space}. $$ As a corollary, we obtain centered DGS at every width with the same exponents, answering a question of Stephens-Davidowitz (SODA 2016).
We introduce Gaussian difference dynamics (GDD), a framework for tracking expected counts and pairwise clustering of vectors through repeated differencing. A closed recursion for the first two counting moments controls these quantities relative to a Gaussian reference, without requiring independence within intermediate lists. Accurate moment bounds let us extract a Gaussian sample by weighted selection, while the weaker bounds needed to establish a shortest vector representation allow us to retain more differences. We perform these transitions on thin spherical shells, where the Gaussian rejection weights can be renormalized at subexponential cost. For batch sampling, we combine this geometry with the double rejection technique of Doulgerakis and Laarhoven to control the joint distribution of outputs while reusing vectors.

item.title: Elliptic Curve Arithmetic for Quantum Cryptanalysis: A Study of Curve25519
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2688
Authors: Yintong Luo, Craig Costello
Summary: Recent quantum resource estimates over prime fields have largely focused on prime order elliptic curves. We implement modern affine circuit techniques on the widely deployed composite order curve, Curve25519, and obtain a scalar circuit using 47,199,530 CCX gates and 1,189 peak logical qubits. This uses approximately 35% and 18% fewer gates than Schrottenloher's published space- and gate-optimized secp256k1 circuits, respectively. We separate three contributions. First, we apply established arithmetic and signed table techniques to Curve25519. In a comparison using the same arithmetic framework and signed half tables, its field and subgroup parameters, together with the chosen GCD iteration budgets, save 2,218,944 CCX gates relative to secp256k1. Second, we adapt odd signed digit recoding to quantum windows using fixed output translations. This saves a further 15,204 CCX gates and also applies to prime order curves. Third, we combine nonzero digits with a fixed 8-torsion offset point to keep the accumulator outside the lookup points' subgroup. With zero slope support and exact field arithmetic, this yields an exception-free addition schedule and nonzero denominators during slope uncomputation, without additional quantum point additions. Our counts include the full scalar schedule, lookup and cleanup. The corresponding implementation uses truncated arithmetic and heuristic GCD budgets, and excludes Fourier rotation synthesis and classical recovery.

item.title: Penalty Deposits For Discrete Logarithms
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2687
Authors: Francisco Vial-Prado, Louis Goubin
Summary: We propose a technique that allows a trusted party in some protocol to attach deposits to their own secrets, without impacting security, and convincing other parties using zero-knowledge proofs. The rationale is that, should this party compromise the protocol by blundering or revealing its secrets, they lose the attached deposit to attackers. As a result, stakeholders gain confidence on how this trusted party operates, and breaches become public as soon as deposits are claimed. We formalize this technique and related security notions, provide two practical constructions in generic discrete logarithm groups, and analyze its application to ECDLP-based protocols.

item.title: Provable Recovery from Integer Quotients: Improved Bounds for Nonlinear Hidden Number Problems
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2686
Authors: Taehun Kang, Changmin Lee
Summary: The hidden number problem (HNP) asks whether a secret can be recovered from partial information about values linked to it by known algebraic relations. In cryptosystems where partial information about secret values or internal randomness is leaked across various scenarios, HNP techniques provide a foundational framework for security analysis and key-recovery attacks. For some HNPs with nonlinear relations, provable polynomial-time recovery guarantees have long remained unimproved, requiring a substantial fraction of the leading bits.
We extend the provable recovery ranges for the modular inversion HNP (MIHNP), elliptic curve HNP (EC-HNP), and HNP with hidden multipliers (HNPHM), all modulo a prime $p$. For any sufficiently small constant $\varepsilon > 0$, we increase the tolerable fraction of unrevealed lower bits: for MIHNP, from $1/3-\varepsilon$ to $1/2-\varepsilon$; for EC-HNP, from $1/6-\varepsilon$ to $1/5-\varepsilon$; and for HNPHM, from $1/5-\varepsilon$ to $1/3-\varepsilon$.
Our algorithm constructs polynomials that vanish modulo $p$ at the unrevealed lower bits, and reduces recovery to bounding their possible integer quotients by $p$ over the candidate range. While such a search can branch in general, we exploit the algebraic relations of each problem to prove that the expected search cost remains polynomial in $\log p$ over randomly sampled inputs. On every valid input, the algorithm returns the exact set of consistent secrets, achieving unique recovery with probability $1-o(1)$ as $p \to \infty$ for every fixed secret.

item.title: Quasi-polynomial time algorithms for block basis reduction of linear codes
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2685
Authors: Kolesnikov N.S., Novoselov S.A.
Summary: The block code basis reduction algorithm (BKZ) proposed by Ghentiyala and Stephens-Davidowitz requires an exponential number of calls to the minimum weight codeword (MWC) oracle according to the weak complexity bounds established in the original paper. In almost all cases these bounds are worse than plain enumeration of codewords, despite the fact that in practice the algorithm works much better. In this work we propose block code basis reduction algorithms with polynomial and quasi-polynomial complexity for fixed $\beta$. Our algorithms are relaxations and modifications of the original algorithm.
