First, we show that the truncated version of the BKZ algorithm requires heuristic quasi-polynomial time of calls to MWC-oracle with the same basis quality as in the full BKZ algorithm. Second, we add some weak restrictions on the code basis that enables the algorithm to run in polynomial number of calls to the oracle. Third, we introduce the DeepBKZ algorithm which is adapted from lattice reduction. Under some relaxations (analogs of PotBKZ from the lattices) it also runs in quasi-polynomial number of calls to the MWC-oracle. We provide an implementation of proposed algorithms which is capable to process block sizes $2-24$ and more. Based on this implementation, we provide concrete complexity estimates and an analysis of the approximation factors achieved for the low-weight codeword problem on random linear codes.

item.title: SoK: Multiple Concurrent Proposer Blockchains
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2684
Authors: Benjamin Marsh, Alejandro Ranchal-Pedrosa, Max Resnick
Summary: Multiple concurrent proposer (MCP) protocols let several parties contribute transactions to the same ledger update. They can distribute communication and reduce one proposer's control over inclusion and order, but these benefits depend on how the contributions are combined. We describe a common architecture from transaction receipt through proposal formation, agreement, data recovery, ordering, execution, and state finality. Within it, we identify four direct MCP families: fixed proposal vectors, selected proposal collections, persistent proposal streams, and causal proposal DAGs. We compare them with constrained assembly, where several parties restrict a block assembled by one party. Across 39 configurations, we distinguish agreement and progress from service for a particular transaction, and compare hiding, ordering, communication, throughput, and latency at explicitly named endpoints. The comparison shows why additional proposers alone do not guarantee inclusion, why hiding does not settle who can react last, and why parallel disseminations need not improve useful execution. It also identifies the recovery, payment, and organizational assumptions needed to turn independent proposal rights into reliable transaction service.

item.title: Stop Calling Them Provers: The Case for Calling ProVerif and Tamarin Symbolic Protocol Analyzers
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2683
Authors: Nadim Kobeissi
Summary: A claim that a cryptographic protocol has been proved secure depends on the theory, the analysis software, the protocol model, and the security property being checked. I examine each of these for ProVerif and Tamarin. An audit of their published soundness arguments finds false statements, missing proofs, and gaps between the procedures justified on paper and those the tools run. I also reproduce previously reported bugs that cause Tamarin to accept false claims about the submitted models. ProVerif supplies no certificate for its full analysis, while Tamarin replays its proof tree with its own solver, leaving the correctness of that code to be trusted.
A correct symbolic result can still fall short of the security claim made for a protocol. Models can omit behavior in parsers and state machines; secrecy queries can allow information to leak; and equations for cryptographic primitives need justification before they support computational guarantees. Better models, stronger queries and computational soundness arguments can address these problems, but someone must establish that they apply to the protocol at hand.
For these reasons and more, I argue that calling ProVerif and Tamarin "provers" is misleading: we should call them symbolic protocol analyzers and report their results with the models, assumptions and evidence that support them. They remain useful for finding attacks and establishing symbolic properties, including for unbounded sessions.

item.title: A Quantitative Evaluation of Constant-Time Analysis Tools
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2682
Authors: Zhenzhi Lai, Zhiyuan Zhang, Tian Qiu, Van-Thuan Pham, Udaya Parampalli
Summary: The constant-time programming policy protects cryptographic code from timing side-channels. However, writing constant-time code remains challenging even for experienced developers. Therefore, over 50 CT analysis tools have been published to help them identify constant-time violations. While several studies have examined those tools, they predominantly rely on qualitative observations and case studies, rather than quantitative assessments. Therefore, we present AutoBench-CT, a modular benchmark that manually verified per-violation ground truths across 64 cryptographic tasks and the first unified quantitative metrics to quantify the Operational Performance, Detection Quality, and Usability for seven such tools. With the results, we quantitatively show why CT-grind, the first tool published in 2010, is still the most popular tool in the wild. Based on the quantitative findings, we further provide new insights into recurring limitations across tools and propose a composite pipeline to maximize the security guarantees of constant-timeness in practice.

item.title: Improving Code Rate and Query Complexity for the Ligero-IOP System
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2681
Authors: Ignacio Cascudo, Carmit Hazay, Muthu Venkitasubramaniam
Summary: This work presents two main contributions to the analysis and design of Ligero-style zero-knowledge proof systems. First, we analyze the original Ligero IOP in the list-decoding regime and show that mutual correlated agreement suffices to obtain improved soundness guarantees and lower query complexity, without modifying the protocol. Second, we propose a new variant of Ligero that incorporates out-of-domain sampling, leading to further soundness improvements and enabling Reed--Solomon code rates above $1/2$. The new protocol preserves the constant-round structure of the Ligero IOP and its compatibility with memory-efficient proving, while achieving perfect honest-verifier zero knowledge.

item.title: (Balanced) Boolean Functions on 375 Variables with Nonlinearity Exceeding the Patterson-Wiedemann Direct-Sum Bound
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2680
Authors: Deng Tang, Subhamoy Maitra
Summary: Patterson and Wiedemann [IEEE-IT 1983] constructed Boolean functions on 15 variables with nonlinearity 16276, which is strictly greater than the bent concatenation bound. Taking their direct sum with a bent function gives nonlinearity $2^{n-1}-27\cdot2^{(n-11)/2}$ for every odd $n\ge15$. Much later, Schmidt [JCT-A 2019] proved that the asymptotic maximum nonlinearity is $2^{n-1}-(1+o(1))2^{n/2-1}$ as $n\to\infty$. In this work, we construct Boolean functions $f$ on 375 variables such that the nonlinearity is greater than $2^{374}-442367\cdot2^{168}=2^{374}-2^{187}+81921\cdot2^{168}$, which exceeds the direct sum of a 15-variable Patterson-Wiedemann function and a bent function on 360 variables. To be specific, the direct sum of a 15-variable Patterson-Wiedemann function and a 360-variable bent function has nonlinearity $2^{374}-2^{187}+20\cdot2^{180}=2^{374} 2^{187}+81920\cdot2^{168}$. Thus our construction improves on this direct-sum value by more than $2^{168}$. Our construction idea is as follows. Let $H$ be the multiplicative subgroup of order $(2^{375}-1)/751$ in $\mathbb F_{2^{375}}^*$. The support of $f$ is the disjoint union of 375 prescribed cosets and a subset $B\subseteq H$. The evaluation of Gauss sums reduces the contribution of the prescribed cosets to a computation of 751 integers. The conditions on $B$ form a $0$-$1$ linear feasibility problem. Using a potential criterion for simultaneous linear constraints, we prove the existence of a single subset $B\subseteq H$ satisfying the constraints at all frequencies. Taking direct sums with bent functions extends the result to every odd $n\ge375$. The support construction does not require balancedness. As a natural follow-up, we also obtain balanced functions with the same strict lower bound by changing the minimum possible number of values, using sampling without replacement. The subsets $B$ and the sets of modified points are obtained by existence proofs.

item.title: Cryptanalysis and Enhancement of VTBSAE: Provably Secure Verifier-Based PAKE Protocols for the Industrial Internet of Things
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2679
Authors: Jiahui Gao, Zhiqiang Zhao, Xuexian Hu
Summary: Verifier‑based password‑authenticated key exchange (PAKE) enables a client and a server to establish high‑entropy session keys from low‑entropy passwords without requiring the server to store plaintext passwords. This asymmetric design reduces the risk that leakage of server‑side credentials directly leads to client impersonation, making verifier‑based PAKE well suited to authentication and session‑key establishment for Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) devices. In this paper, we analyze the recently proposed VTBSAE, a verifier‑based PAKE protocol, and reveal that it fails to provide the claimed resistance against server‑compromise client‑impersonation attacks. To fix this vulnerability, we propose E‑VTBSAEv1. While preserving the lightweight structure of VTBSAE, E‑VTBSAEv1 binds the client‑generated point \(E_{1}\) to fresh server‑side randomness. We also briefly discuss E‑VTBSAEv2 as a challenge‑based variant. We provide a formal security proof for E‑VTBSAEv1 in the random‑oracle model under the CDH assumption, covering AKE security, forward secrecy, and resistance to server‑compromise client‑impersonation attacks after server‑side verifier‑file leakage. We evaluate E‑VTBSAEv1 under two practical deployment settings: a Raspberry Pi 4B server with an AutoDL client, and a Raspberry Pi 4B server with a Raspberry Pi 4B client. The experimental results show that E‑VTBSAEv1 preserves the communication and storage overheads of VTBSAE and achieves runtime performance comparable to that of VTBSAE.

item.title: From Quantum Mechanics to the Hidden Subgroup Problem: an Overview from Finite to Infinite Groups
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2678
Authors: Federico Di Concilio, Ramón Flores, Delaram Kahrobaei, Marialaura Noce
Summary: The Hidden Subgroup Problem (HSP for short) is an important problem in quantum computing and computational group theory, which has connections with several quantum algorithms, including Shor's algorithm for integer factorization and the discrete logarithm problem. The HSP can be stated as follows: given a function on a group that is constant and distinct on cosets of a hidden subgroup, determine the hidden subgroup efficiently. The problem captures the essence of exploiting group structures for computational advantage and provides insights into the power of quantum algorithms over classical approaches. While abelian instances of HSP are well-understood and efficiently solvable using the quantum Fourier transform, non-abelian cases remain challenging and are active areas of research. The goal of this survey is to put together all the basic background needed to understand well the Hidden Subgroup Problem in groups, reviewing recent results and discussing open problems.

item.title: Smoothness of Shortest Isogenies to Frobenius Conjugatess
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2677
Authors: Yi Ouyang, Wei Wei, Zheng Xu
Summary: Let \(E\) be chosen uniformly from the geometric isomorphism classes of supersingular elliptic curves over \(\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p\) and \(\delta_E\) be the minimum degree of isogenies from \(E\) to its Frobenius conjugate \(E^{(p)}\). We establish bounds for the smoothness probability of $\delta_E$ and hence affirm Wesolowski's \(p^{1/3+o(1)}\) attack on the supersingular endomorphism ring problem is unconditional. We also establish a uniform asymptotic formula, with a main term expressed in terms of Dirichlet \(L\)-values, for the probability that a connection isogeny of degree $n$ exists between $E$ and $E^{(p)}$.

item.title: Optimality and Efficiency of Higher-Order Rank-Based Side-Channel Attacks against Inner Product Masking Schemes
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2676
Authors: Haitao Zhan, Wei Cheng, Yuejun Liu, Jingdian Ming, Sylvain Guilley, Yongbin Zhou
Summary: Higher-Order Spearman Coefficient Analysis (HO-SPA) is of particular interest in non-profiling Side-Channel Attacks (SCA) due to its effectiveness against monotonic nonlinear leakage. However, the optimal form, effective order combinations, and performance of HO-SPA (or its variants) remain underexplored. This work systematically revisits HO-SPA in the presence of Boolean Masking (BM) and Inner Product Masking (IPM). Specifically, we propose a new variant of HO-SPA, called HO-ASPA (Higher-Order Adjusted Spearman Coefficient Analysis), and derive the optimal form of HO-ASPA for two-share BM and IPM across a wide range of order combinations under the Hamming weight (HW) leakage model. We first derive the optimal form of HO-ASPA by extending the Spearman Coefficient Analysis to higher-order moments, while preserving the centered-product combination of the share leakages. We then establish an upper bound on the maximal correlation induced by the rank transformation and characterize the relationship between the signal-to-noise ratio and the optimal correlation coefficient in the rank-domain, and extend these analyses to IPM. To enable a fair comparison, we also derive the optimal forms of Higher-Order Correlation Power Analysis (HO-CPA) and HO-ASPA for both BM and IPM under the Least-Significant-Bit (LSB) leakage model. Our analysis highlights a key distinction: unlike HO-CPA, where higher orders often outperform the lowest feasible order, HO-ASPA shows no significant performance gap between higher-order and lower-order attacks. Moreover, under the HW leakage model, our HO-ASPA not only aligns with existing results and succeeds in counteracting the security order amplification, but also significantly outperforms Kruskal-Wallis Analysis (KWA)-based attacks at various order combinations. We further validate the effectiveness of the proposed HO-ASPA through simulated and real-world experimental evaluations.

item.title: High Precision Noise Cleaning for CKKS with Application to Asynchronous Threshold CKKS
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2675
Authors: Zhihao Li, Cheng Hong, Tao Wei
Summary: Noise cleaning in discrete CKKS uses Hermite interpolation to reduce the input error while preserving the encrypted discrete message. Cryptographic applications based on noise flooding require the error after cleaning to be sufficiently small for the added noise to provide statistical hiding without preventing exact recovery. This requirement is more stringent than decryption correctness alone, but the achievable noise reduction is limited by errors introduced during homomorphic evaluation. In particular, key switching and rescaling can dominate the output error even when a higher interpolation order substantially reduces the polynomial residual.
We propose a high precision noise cleaning method for CKKS that preserves encrypted integer messages while attaining a prescribed bound on normalized output noise. We jointly select the cleaning polynomials and evaluation parameters according to a complete error bound that accounts for the input noise and the errors introduced during homomorphic evaluation. By composing Hermite polynomials of lower degree, we can achieve the same output noise bound with a smaller ciphertext modulus and lower evaluation cost than a single higher degree polynomial. In addition, to reduce the ciphertext tensor degree, we construct polynomial representations with noisy auxiliary powers that cancel selected auxiliary error terms. For integer messages, we extract the bits through multi-value functional bootstrapping, then clean and recombine them into a single ciphertext. Finally, we apply high precision noise cleaning to construct an asynchronous threshold CKKS scheme that achieves strong simulation security in the random oracle model.
We implement binary and integer noise cleaning in OpenFHE. For binary messages and a normalized output noise target of $2^{-300}$, the selected composition reduces cleaning time from $9.63$ to $1.54$ seconds compared with a single Hermite evaluation under the same input error bound and security requirements. The composition also requires a smaller input ciphertext modulus and less evaluation key storage. We also evaluate the complete construction on 8 bit integers packed into all $32{,}768$ slots. The maximum measured normalized output noise is below $2^{-300}$ with either leveled digit extraction or functional bootstrapping.
